evidence.fact: Commercial AI skin-analysis tools already scan a face from a photo, detect about 15 skin concerns such as redness, wrinkles and texture, and then generate a personalised product routine with explanations.

Consumer AI skincare apps recommend products based on skin type and explain which ingredient targets which concern, although they state their advice is informational only. The salon version of this task still depends on in-person skin assessment, demonstrating how to apply products and building client trust during the service.

State cosmetology boards regulate skin-care services, meaning the physical treatments, under the license. Makeup demonstrations and product advice are not described as acts only a licensee may perform, so no human sign-off is required to recommend products.
One vendor's AI agent connects to Booqable rental software. It reads live inventory to check availability and can create bookings and look up customers. Staff still handle the physical logistics.
Rently's AI agent on WhatsApp answers questions about availability, pricing and requirements, and records reservations in the rental system. Complex requests and VIP customers go to human staff.
Bookyt's rental chatbot matches a customer's question to the rental offering, asks for any missing details, and points to booking. This covers much of the discussion about type, quality and quantity.
Conversational-commerce AI agents already greet online shoppers proactively, answer questions and recommend products to identify needs. Fin puts the 2026 market at about $10–14B.
Gorgias says proactive AI engagement drove 50% of conversation-driven purchases during BFCM 2025, which shows AI handling the greet-and-qualify step in digital channels. This is vendor data.

Agentic commerce tools such as Salesforce Agentforce Commerce work in digital storefronts. On the shop floor, greeting and reading customers face to face needs physical presence, which a bodiless agent lacks, so its role there is limited to helping staff (product lookup, suggestions).

Microsoft Brand Agents bring the advice a store associate would give into a chat on the retailer's website, including guidance, upselling and cross-selling. Google, OpenAI, Shopify and PayPal are building similar conversational shopping where customers compare and buy in one place.

In stores, AI copilots and voice-headset assistants support human associates by giving them product, inventory and recommendation data in real time. The associate still serves the customer face to face and physically finds the items.

Manhattan Active Omni's Store Associate Agent answers natural-language questions about inventory and customer behavior, so an agent can handle the 'locate or obtain' step through software. Gaps in universal carts, APIs and product data still limit full deployment.

AI travel chatbots and agents already put together information tailored to the traveler's itinerary and nationality. This includes visa and entry rules, transit requirements, local customs and etiquette, so the main step of assembling the information is automated.

No-code AI agents automatically check visa and entry eligibility by nationality and destination and alert users when requirements change. Guidance for travel agents still advises checking AI drafts against official sources.

IATA Timatic gives travel agents passport, visa and health requirements for over 220 countries, online or by API. That makes the authoritative regulation data digitally reachable, so an agent can send it to the customer by email or in a document instead of handing over a printed brochure.

Vendor pages describe AI agents that run program enrollment from start to finish. They ask qualifying questions, send eligible applicants on to enrollment, offer waitlists or other programs to the rest, and follow up automatically by email or SMS. These are marketing claims and have not been independently checked.

The same vendor offers agents for government health-program enrollment. They pre-screen applicants on household income, family size and participation in other programs, and they collect registration details.

A guide on automating financial aid recommends that AI handle screening, flagging, document requests and status outreach, while humans make the final eligibility or award decisions. Low-confidence cases should go to a human, and every automated decision should be logged.

AI tools such as S7 PLC Buddy, which uses Claude, can read live PLC diagnostics over the network and suggest likely causes. The vendor notes that the operational data agents need is spread across separate systems like SCADA, historians and fleet software.
Agent products for field technicians combine live readings, error logs and maintenance history to help with troubleshooting, but a technician still does the hands-on work.

Under NFPA 70E, touching energized parts with probes or test equipment counts as energized work. It must be done by a qualified person physically present with the right PPE, so diagnosing with meters and scopes needs someone on site.

Vendor pages say hotel revenue-management systems (RoomPriceGenie, PricingService.ai, RoomRaccoon/Pricepoint) set room rates on their own from competitor prices, booking pace and occupancy, push them to the PMS and channel manager, and offer an autopilot mode. These are vendor claims, not independent results.

Hotel budgeting tools such as Otelier TruePlan pull actuals from PMS, POS and accounting systems and use pre-built drivers to cut budget build time. Building the budget still needs input from department heads, and the owner or GM must approve how funds are split between departments.
Vendor buyer's guides say AI budgeting and forecasting software automates driver-based forecasts and budget updates. I found no evidence of fully autonomous budget approval or fund allocation.

Code for America and Anthropic built a SNAP Policy Navigator that answers policy questions with cited sources, but the eligibility decision stays with humans. This shows AI can handle the research and interpretation steps of eligibility policy work.

Research on Rules as Code found that LLMs are useful for summarizing and interpreting SNAP and Medicaid policy but not ideal for implementing strict formulas such as benefit calculations, so humans still need to review the work.
Human service agency standards give policy-setting responsibility to the volunteer board, so deciding policy and being accountable for it stays with people.
O*NET lists 'confer with customer representatives to review schematics and answer questions pertaining to installation of systems' as a task of Mechanical Drafters (17-3013.00).

AI tools in 2026 index CAD files, PDFs and scanned drawings and return source-cited answers to technical questions. This automates retrieval and drafting of answers, but vendors describe these as tools for internal engineering teams, not as agents that hold customer meetings on their own.

Electrical CAD software (WSCAD ELECTRIX AI 2026) has built-in assistants that answer technical installation questions such as wire sizing. This supports partial automation of answering questions about schematics.

State environmental agencies increasingly run permitting and public notices through electronic systems. Louisiana's 2026 SB 99 gives emailed and electronic notices the same legal weight as mailed ones. An agent can handle these digital channels.

RCRA permit and closure documents have to be placed in publicly accessible locations near the facility or at agency offices, and notices go out to facility mailing lists. Some distribution is still on paper or in person.
Some state programs, such as Maryland's, still ask for hard copies and use mail alongside email. This leaves physical sub-steps for a human, or for a print-and-mail service.

Integrated library systems already handle circulation, patron, inventory and serials records and produce reports in software, so an agent with access to the ILS could compile and update these records through the software itself.
Automated circulation modules keep transaction records, overdue notices, item status (lost, missing, withdrawn), stock verification and report generation, so much of the record-keeping is digital.

Physical stock-taking and equipment checks are still done with handheld RFID readers or shelf scanning. That is the physical input a human (or robot) has to supply before the records can be checked against what is on the shelves.

AI agents bought a Czech ad campaign from start to finish, linking Omnicom Media and publisher MAFRA through an MCP gateway and the Ad Context Protocol (AdCP). This is the vendor's own account and has not been independently checked.

At Cannes 2026, Yahoo DSP's Agent Network, TikTok's Symphony Agent and others launched agents that buy and sell ads. A PubMatic executive warned that reliability problems would be common in agent-run media buying.
AdCP was launched in October 2025 with a Media Buy protocol built on MCP. In the first live agent-run media buy, a human approved the purchase.

Manufacturer services such as Sysmex BeyondCare and Ortho's Remote Monitoring Center already do remote calibration, QC monitoring and predictive alerts. Software can therefore take over the data side (QC trend review, scheduling, alerting), but a human still loads calibrators and reagents and does the hands-on maintenance on site.

A clinical-analyzer QC patent describes analyzers sending calibration and QC data and alarms over a network to manufacturer service servers for statistical analysis. This means only some data and diagnostic sub-steps can be done remotely.

CLIA 42 CFR 493.1255 requires labs to perform and document calibration verification at least every 6 months and after major preventive maintenance. CMS surveys cite labs that miss this, so qualified lab personnel remain accountable.

Pharmacy software such as Cegedim Pharmacy Manager's 'Fast Labelling' already fills in the patient, product, directions and quantity from an electronic prescription, so most label preparation is software-driven typing and printing. An agent using the computer could do the remaining data entry and trigger the print.

In pharmacy automation such as Parata Max, integrated printers already produce labels with patient details, medication, dosage instructions, barcodes and regulatory data without anyone typing them. Someone still has to handle the printed label and attach it to the container.

State rules (for example Arizona R4-23-1104 and Mississippi Art. XL) let technicians type and print labels but require a pharmacist to verify their accuracy and hold that pharmacist responsible for the data entered. A human review step therefore stays in place.

Kitchen display systems already pace items by cook time so they reach the expo window together. For example, a 20-minute steak is fired before a 12-minute salmon, and shorter-cook items are held back. This automates the scheduling part of the task.

Toast POS has a 'fire by prep time' item-pacing setting that sends items to stations based on their cook times. It relies on configured cook times, not on what is actually happening at the grill, so the cook still adjusts in real time.
KDS vendors offer course pacing, fire timing and course-hold functions with set gaps between courses, which shows the sequencing logic can be done in software.

Vendors say their bar ID-scanning software runs more than 75 automated checks on each ID and flags suspicious documents. They claim it detects up to 95% of fake IDs when paired with UV/IR/hologram hardware. These are vendor claims with no independent testing found.

Some systems combine document scanning with AI facial age estimation (Yoti) to catch good fakes. Software can do the authenticity and age-calculation steps, but someone still has to take the physical card and match the face to the photo at the bar.

States such as California require ID checkers to complete Responsible Beverage Service training. Their 'diligent inspection' defense, and North Carolina's point-of-sale carding with server liability, put legal responsibility on a human server.

By 2026, voice AI agents (SoundHound at Red Lobster and Five Guys, plus Aldelo's POS voice agent) take restaurant phone and drive-thru orders end to end and send them to the POS. However, accuracy failures have occurred, including McDonald's ending its IBM order-taking test in 2024.

With QR-code table ordering, diners browse, order and pay on their phones and the order goes straight to the kitchen and POS. Some restaurants have dropped servers for order-taking, but most keep staff in a hybrid model.
Vendors describe QR or app ordering as removing the server's job of bringing menus and taking orders. Staff are still needed at the table to deliver food and help guests.

Flipdish's AI phone agent takes orders and suggests specials, sides and drinks to callers, then sends confirmed orders to the POS. This shows AI can tell customers about specials over remote channels.
Pos Dish's QR and digital menus feature seasonal specials and new dishes, so table-side digital channels can carry the specials information instead of a server.
Dynamu AI, an 'AI waiter' for full-service dine-in restaurants reached by QR code, is still in early pilots. Spoken, in-person delivery at the table still mostly needs a human server.

Washoe County, Nevada licensing rules say a caregiver who counts toward the staff-to-child ratio must be physically in the room with the child, close enough to step in. Maine requires that all children can be seen or heard at all times and that sleeping children are checked in person every 30 minutes.

State licensing rules, such as Arizona's, set required staff-to-children ratios by age (1:5 for infants) that count only qualified human staff, and programs get cited when ratios or supervision fall short.
Childcare software such as Brightwheel handles side admin work: daily reports to parents, attendance and billing. The care itself is not done in software.

CDC guidance says sterilizing and sanitizing are hands-on jobs: washing bottles after every feeding, boiling or soaking items, or using a dishwasher's sanitize cycle, then air-drying them. A software-only agent can't do any of this.

Childcare standards (Caring for Our Children / Head Start) say caregivers must mix formula following the parent's or manufacturer's instructions and label bottles with the child's name and the date and time. All of these are physical steps done by staff, so AI could at most help look up guidance.
To prepare formula safely you have to boil water, mix by shaking or swirling, and refrigerate bottles and throw them out on time. Every step means handling the bottles directly.

AI activity planners such as Kidtivity Lab and Taskade's Children's Activity Planner can generate age-appropriate games, crafts and activity plans. That covers only the planning step, not running the activities.
Taskade offers a customizable agent that builds children's activity plans from a child's age, interests and learning style. A caregiver still has to carry out the plan.

Nanny work means caring for children in person and without supervision, which is why it needs vetting (for example a UK Enhanced DBS check). Running games, sports, walks and play dates needs a physically present, trusted caregiver.

The chore and reward apps I found (FamilyPoints, NeatKid and others) only let parents assign chores and track points or stars. A human still has to watch the child and give the praise; none of these apps does it on its own.

NeatKid includes positive-reinforcement features, but the praise is digital and gated by parents. Software can support the task (chore lists, tracking), while praising a child at the moment of the behavior requires a person who is physically present.

Nanny licensing rules differ by jurisdiction and usually cover the care setting and background checks. None of the sources I found requires a licensed human to assign chores or praise behavior, so legal accountability is not the main barrier.
Computer-vision produce recognition is sold for self-checkout (Toshiba ELERA, Diebold Nixdorf pilot at Aldi Süd). It identifies the item, but a person still has to put the produce on the scale.
Vision systems recognize produce and price it from the measured weight. The price calculation is already automated by the scale and POS system, so AI adds very little to it.
Checkout scales used for direct sale to consumers must be NTEP-approved and legal for trade. This rule covers the device, not a requirement for a human operator.

Cash-recycler and smart-safe software tracks cash and coin levels in real time for each till and clerk, and alerts managers when levels need attention. This automates the cash-monitoring step, but someone still has to carry cash to the till.
Avivatech's XpressControl dashboard shows cash on hand by cashier, till and location, and automatically alerts users to issues that need fixing.

Computer-vision queue systems count customers at checkout lanes and alert managers to open lanes when lines pass a set limit. This automates spotting staffing gaps, but a person still has to staff the lane. These claims come from vendors and have not been independently checked.

Benevity says its certified Workday integration automates payroll giving and cuts internal admin work. Third-party listings say it handles payroll-deduction donations and automatic corporate matching.
In January 2026 ADP launched Assist Agents that plan and act across HR and payroll workflows, with humans keeping oversight.
QuickBooks' Payroll Agent drafts pay runs and journal entries for wages, taxes and benefits for a human to approve. It does not run payroll by itself.
Monitor ERP's Agent automatically sends regular reports, such as order inflow and sales statistics, to the right employees in Excel or PDF format.
The OutSystems Sales Reporting Agent answers sales questions in plain language using the Customer, Order, Product and Supplier data stored in OutSystems.
The Infosys order management app on SAP uses agentic AI to give insights on order status, fulfillment performance, exceptions and reconciliation.

Motorola Solutions' Assist AI for 911 (expanded June 2026) streams live 911 audio, call summaries and transcripts to field units through CAD and mobile apps, and adds real-time translation. This automates passing information from callers to responders, but dispatchers still run it.

AI call takers handle non-emergency calls in Minnesota PSAPs. In Dakota County, AI redirected about 33% of calls in 2025. Emergency radio traffic and inter-agency relay are still done by human telecommunicators.

Some states require each PSAP calltaker or dispatcher position to be staffed by a person who has completed approved telecommunicator training (e.g., New Jersey, Florida, North Carolina). That implies a human must perform the work, though there is no single national standard.

A FEMA posting for a mobile communications vehicle job lists movement planning, operating and maintaining the vehicle, pre-trip inspections, and setting up and maintaining communications equipment. It asks for the ability to safely operate large commercial-size vehicles under federal and state rules. This is hands-on physical work, and only the planning, record-keeping and IT troubleshooting can be done in software.
A county telecommunicator posting says some duties are done outdoors in a communications trailer, so the worker has to be there in person.

Canadian Job Bank descriptions of emergency communications officers include operating radio and telecommunication equipment and coordinating vehicles and personnel. These are tasks done at a console, which software can help with but not physically carry out.

Canva Magic Design creates layout options from a text prompt or an uploaded image. A 2026 update reportedly lets its AI resize, recolor and adjust layouts on its own, so agents can draft sample layouts from start to finish. A person still reviews the result for brand fit and typography.
Canva Magic Layers (March 2026) turns flat designs into editable layered layouts, which supports automated layout revision.
Desktop publishing operators are not a regulated occupation in Canada, and no professional licence is needed to prepare layouts. The work is done entirely in software, with no physical step.

Flooring estimating software such as Measure Square can automatically create carpet cut sheets. It optimizes seam placement, layout direction, waste, roll width and pattern-repeat allowances, so the planning that follows the floor sketch can be done digitally.
Users still adjust the software's cuts by hand, and reviewers say moving cuts is clunky and some calculations are unreliable. A human has to check the plan before carpet is cut.

The main work is physical: rolling out the carpet, measuring and marking it on site, and cutting it with a carpet knife. An agent with no body or robotics cannot do these steps, so it can only help with the cut plan. No licence or sign-off requirement applies to this step.
AI maintenance copilots search manuals, work-order history and procedures to give troubleshooting guidance to technicians. The technician still does the physical repair.
Vendor AI assistants are sold as technician aids, claiming faster issue resolution and shorter mean time to repair. They do not carry out repairs on their own.
Some states, such as Hawaii, require at least a maintenance electrician's licence for electrical maintenance work and a journey worker or master plumber licence for plumbing work.

In O*NET, Packers and Packagers, Hand (53-7064.00) is manual work. Related tasks include moving products and orders by hand and placing them on conveyors or loading docks. My search found no O*NET task with the exact wording 'transport packages to customers' vehicles', so the task was rated as given.

The task means physically carrying or wheeling packages to a customer's vehicle. The reference AI agents have no body or robotics, so they could at most help with small digital steps like order lookup or pickup notifications. Not checked by search; inferred from the task and the agent definition.

Vendor sources describe AI-moderated and synthetic-audience concept testing that can run many consumer interviews at once and finish in hours instead of weeks. These are marketing claims and have not been independently verified.
By 2026, agentic project-management tools such as ClickUp, Wrike, Notion and Linear handle triage, spec drafting, tracking and reporting, but they hand key decisions back to humans at defined points.
A 2026 systematic review found that AI agents can simulate project-manager roles for planning and progress tracking, while humans keep the final decisions.

Funeral homes usually notify the Social Security Administration (SSA) of the death and help with SSA and VA burial paperwork. Survivors must apply themselves for the $255 lump-sum payment and for monthly survivor benefits. The work is mostly finding out who is eligible and explaining the rules, which is document and information work an agent can do from the case details.

The VA cannot pay DIC, survivor pension or burial allowance until the death is recorded in its system, and families need the DD-214. These are clear, rule-based eligibility checks that an agent could build into a personalized benefits summary.

Funeral software already offers aftercare and case-management modules, and some store burial claims and Social Security forms. The talk itself usually happens face to face with grieving families during the arrangement conference, so a person still delivers the information and checks it.

Commercial survey software (Carlson Survey, MicroSurvey CAD, Geo-plus VisionCogo) already handles COGO, traverse and least-squares adjustment, and lot closure checks. Leica Cyclone II TOPO and VisionLidar find ground points and classify point clouds automatically. An agent that can operate these tools could do most of the number-crunching.

An industry article says AI handles numeric data well but struggles with historical, vague or contradictory boundary descriptions, and that automated output must be checked against known benchmarks. That means a human still has to review the work, especially for property lines.
In states such as Oregon, Maryland and Oklahoma, surveying documents have to be signed and sealed by a licensed surveyor who is in responsible charge of the work.

SLB says its AI-enabled digital tools automated workover candidate screening and ranking at PGN Saka. It reports an 89% cut in selection time, with review moving from yearly to weekly across 196 completions. These figures come from the vendor.
A commercial AI tool is marketed as ranking every well in a portfolio by expected intervention ROI. This is vendor marketing, not independent evidence of performance.

In these BLM sundry examples, workover and plugging work needs prior regulator approval of a sundry notice that the operator's representative signs. The search found no rule requiring a PE stamp on a workover program, though the sources are scattered office-level examples rather than a statewide rule. In practice, operators keep an engineer accountable for the final rework design and spending.
O*NET lists fitting orthopedic braces, prostheses and supportive devices as a task for physical therapist aides, who work under close supervision of a PT or PTA and do only delegated, routine tasks.
An Illinois state position description requires aides to work under direct supervision of a PT or PTA. This shows the work is supervised, hands-on clinical care.

Phone-based 3D scanning apps such as SnugFit, Thuasne3D and SpinalTech3D take body scans for designing custom orthoses. A human still holds the device, and none of the apps do the physical fitting or adjust the fit on the patient.
O*NET lists packing body orifices with cotton soaked in embalming fluid as a hands-on embalmer task done directly on the body.
In Wisconsin, only a licensed, registered embalmer may embalm a body, and only in approved places such as licensed funeral establishments or hospitals.
Hawaii's rules let an apprentice embalm only in the presence of, and under the direction of, a licensed embalmer.
In Louisiana, funeral homes enter death records in the LEERS online system and can get and print burial transit permits there at any hour. This is browser work an agent could do.

In Massachusetts' default opt-out setup, a local burial agent must review the record and assign permit information before the permit can be printed. That means a human checkpoint outside the agent's control.

Passare's funeral software connects directly to Pennsylvania's death registration system through an API. Software already handles the filing step, but a credentialed funeral director still has to sign the record.

AI masonry takeoff tools (e.g., Civils.ai, Oncenter Takeoff Boost) measure block/brick wall runs, deduct openings and count units directly from PDF drawings; vendor claims cut takeoff time by up to 95%.

A 2026 independent study of Togal AI on a live commercial project found near-perfect count accuracy but consistent underestimation of area quantities, especially on exterior finishes, and concluded that estimator oversight remains essential.
Togal's own help documentation recommends treating automated takeoff results as a starting point to review before finalizing.

O*NET lists this as a core hands-on task for Helpers--Electricians (47-3013.00): operating cutting torches and welding equipment on conduit and metal components. The occupation is described as using, supplying or holding materials and tools.

Related task entries are also manual conduit work: threading conduit ends, connecting couplings, making support brackets with hand tools, and measuring, cutting and bending wire and conduit. A software-only agent with no body cannot do any of this. At most it could look up weld settings or read drawings, which is a small share of the time.
Plumber helpers cut and thread pipe with pipe cutters, cutting torches and threading machines, and help lift and position objects on site.
A posting requires helpers to carry up to 75 lbs and lift up to 100 lbs, mostly while standing or walking.
Canadian guidance lists manual material handling, bending and repetitive motion as the core physical demands of the helper job.

Robots that mark roads, such as Civ Robotics' CivDash, exist, but they are dedicated hardware run remotely from a safety truck. A software-only AI agent cannot do this work. It could only help with minor planning or record-keeping.

Most robots so far only do layout and pre-marking. Final thermoplastic marking, heated to about 400°F, still uses crews with truck-mounted or hand equipment. Systems like RoadPrintz still need an operator in the truck.

Under the MUTCD, pavement marking happens on site in work zones. The work has to be staged with temporary traffic control, and workers with traffic-control duties must be trained. All of this needs people physically present on the road.

Wisconsin DOT's maintenance manual says crews set snow-fence posts in the field before the ground freezes, then hang the fencing taut after it freezes, 35 times the fence height from the shoulder edge. This is hands-on fieldwork.
In a Utah DOT case study, a crew of three trained workers placed about 1,000 ft of fence in an 8-hour shift. The work is manual labour on site, and an agent without a body cannot do it.
MnDOT employees built a permanent 1,500-ft woven snow fence by hand after an agreement with the landowners. Only the planning and coordination around it is digital.

Manufacturing execution system (MES) recipe-management software stores recipe steps and parameter values, such as oven temperature settings, and flags when operators depart from them. This means pulling cook parameters from recipes and work orders can be done digitally.
Recipes are often stored on, or editable only through, the equipment controller on the plant floor. An agent may therefore not be able to reach those systems or paper work orders.

Under 21 CFR 113/114, thermal-processing operators must work under the supervision of a supervisor certified through the Better Process Control School, and scheduled processes must be set by a qualified person. Human oversight stays in place, but no one has to sign for the act of reading the recipe itself.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Cleaners of Vehicles and Equipment (53-7061.00). The work is done by hand: sweeping, shoveling or vacuuming debris and scrap into containers, then carrying the containers out of work areas. A software-only agent with no body cannot do any of it.

The occupation's other tasks use physical tools and materials such as water, cleaning agents, brushes, cloths, hoses and vacuums. This confirms the job requires being on site and handling things physically.

Disney California Adventure tested automated entry gates where guests tap MagicBand+ or tickets themselves and the gate opens after the ticket is scanned and a photo is taken or checked. This replaces an attendant's handheld scanner, but it is fixed gate hardware, not a software AI agent.
Theme park turnstile vendors sell sensor-based speed gates tied to ticketing systems. The digital checking step is automated, but the gates and readers are physical equipment at the entrance.

Walt Disney World entrances have used RFID ticket readers with a fingerprint scanner. Ticket checking can be automated through on-site devices, yet collecting or punching tickets and admitting or stopping patrons still happens in person.

Job postings list installing pipes, HVAC ducts, flashing, rain gutters and furnace casings as a core hands-on task. The work also includes reading blueprints and fastening seams on site, which needs a person physically there.
Installation work includes laying out and installing gutters, downspouts, ducts and flashing. Only small paperwork steps, such as estimating materials and labour hours, could be done in software.
Some employers and jurisdictions require a journeyman sheet metal worker licence or a trade certificate to do this work.

Servicing a hub axle is hands-on work. The mechanic holds the cone with a cone wrench, loosens the locknut, unscrews the cone, catches the loose bearings, regreases and reassembles the hub, then sets bearing play by feel. An agent without a body can do none of this, and its only help would be to look up procedures or specs.
The work uses physical tools such as cone wrenches, locknut wrenches, an axle vise, tweezers, degreaser and grease.
No government license is generally required for bicycle mechanics. Certification is voluntary, through bodies such as UBI and BBI, so accountability is not a barrier.

A RAND survey covered by District Administration found nearly 60% of K-12 principals use AI tools for work. Drafting communications such as newsletters, emails and staff memos is the most common use, and administrators still review the output.

Apptegy's school newsletter builder has a 'Write with AI' drafting feature and sends newsletters digitally under district-level control. This automates both writing and distribution of promotional material.
An ESD 112 school communications guide recommends using AI to draft newsletters while keeping the district's voice, so human review is still expected before publishing.

Workday Adaptive Planning, a common higher-education planning platform, lists an AI Planning Agent and uses machine learning for predictive forecasts. This means much of the forecasting, modeling and report production can be automated.
University boards delegate to the CFO the authority and responsibility to set up and manage the budget and accounting system. Accountability stays with named human officers.
The Comptroller prepares the annual financial statements under GAAP, an independent CPA audits them, and the Trustees must approve them. Human sign-off and review are required before use.

Sakana AI's 'The AI Scientist' (Nature, March 2026) runs a pipeline that analyses data, drafts the full manuscript and reviews its own work. One of its papers passed first-round peer review at a workshop, which shows that drafting a write-up of findings can be delegated end to end.
A May 2026 survey found that frontier LLMs still make up results, miss hidden errors and judge novelty poorly, so a human still has to review and correct the work before it is published.
ICMJE, COPE and major publishers do not allow AI tools to be listed as authors. Human authors must approve the final manuscript and take responsibility for its integrity.

Current AI use for supervising teaching assistants is limited to pilots and human-in-the-loop tools. Examples are AI-built onboarding modules for TAs and 'shadow grading' agents that work alongside instructors. Mentoring and research guidance stay with the human supervisor.
University policy makes the faculty supervisor the instructor of record for an internship, and that person assigns the grade.
The faculty supervisor has the ultimate responsibility for evaluating students' internship or practicum work, even when a sponsor's representative oversees the student day to day.

Korinek's NBER Working Paper 34202 (2025) shows AI agents helping at every stage of economic research, from background research to coding and analysis. These are sub-steps an agent can prepare before or after meetings with colleagues.

Agentic co-scientist systems such as Google's generate, critique and refine hypotheses, but they support research that humans lead. They do not stand in for the interpersonal back-and-forth between colleagues.
Academic forums in 2026 warn against relying on agents for every decision, so collaborative judgement and agreement stay with the faculty members.

Campus bookstore adoption portals such as Barnes & Noble's Adoption & Insight Portal let faculty search by ISBN, re-adopt materials in one click, and compare options across price ranges, including OER. These are all digital steps that a computer-use agent could carry out.
The Akademos Adoption & Analytics Portal includes a recommendation engine that suggests other high-quality, low-cost options. That means software already handles part of the selection work.

Adoption systems such as Follett Discover sit behind campus single sign-on and Canvas or Blackboard, and have adoption deadlines. An agent therefore needs the instructor's credentials, and the instructor still has to make the final decision about which texts fit the course.

2026 researcher tooling already does the main sub-steps: Semantic Scholar AI and Elicit find and group literature, and Zotero MCP and paper-search MCP servers let agents search for and manage references.

Reading lists made by AI still need human checking: the Chicago Sun-Times printed a summer list where 10 of 15 books were invented, and librarians report many hallucinated citations. A faculty member still has to review the list before assigning it.

Studies report high rates of invented or wrong references in AI-assisted literature work (about two-thirds in one GPT-4o study), so checking each item against library catalogs is an essential step, along with the instructor's judgment on whether a work suits the course.

University of Duisburg-Essen tested Claude Opus 4.6 as an assistive grader on 18 written IHK vocational exams in summer 2025. It matched the human grade exactly in 14 cases, was one grade off in the other 4, and never changed a pass/fail result. The researchers say high-stakes use still needs validation and recommend combining digital tests with in-person exams. No 2026 study was found of AI scoring hands-on vocational performance tests.

NYU Stern's voice-AI system ran personalized oral exams for two undergraduate cohorts of 36 and 37 students, and LLMs graded the transcripts for under $1 per exam. It had flaws: it sometimes asked several questions at once, did not randomize topics, and its cloned professor voice sounded harsh.

Gradescope's AI groups similar answers on handwritten or digital exams, with OCR handling handwriting, so instructors can grade in batches. Instructors still review the groups and apply the rubrics, so the human stays in the loop.

MagicSchool offers an IEP Generator and an Accommodation Suggestion Generator for special education teachers. The vendor says to review the output closely before using it and to treat it as suggestions only. So an agent can draft strategies end to end, but a teacher still has to review them.

Guides for educators warn that AI does not know the individual student. They say its strategy and accommodation drafts need the teacher to add baseline data, context and professional judgment. This depends on observing the student and on student records that districts often restrict.

Under IDEA, special education teachers need a bachelor's degree and full state special education certification. Emergency or provisional credentials do not qualify. A licensed human is therefore responsible for carrying out the strategies with students in the classroom.

MagicSchool AI's Lesson Plan Generator builds a plan from grade, subject, topic and state or Common Core standards. It also has tools for differentiation and IEP accommodations, so it can produce written lesson-prep documents.
A review of EduAide.AI says complex IEP differentiation for students with severe learning needs still needs a human specialist, which supports keeping a teacher review step.
A university guide on AI in education advises checking AI-generated material before using it with students because the output can be biased or incorrect.
Terrazzo workers partly press metal divider strips into the wet sandy concrete underbed before it sets. This is hands-on manual work done on site.
NTMA guidance says strips must be anchored well into the cement/sand underbed so they cannot move. This calls for physical setting and judging on the floor.

Federal specs require strips set with tight butt joints, true and square, held with cement mortar, and laid out following the drawing pattern. An AI could at most help interpret the layout from the drawings.

The only real example of a driverless refuse truck is Volvo's trial with Renova in Sweden around 2016–2017, which used lidar and GPS on a purpose-built vehicle. That is robotics, not a software-only agent. The search found no 2026 deployment of a fully driverless garbage truck; the 2026 'automated collection' programs use mechanical arms, and a human still drives.
Automated side-loading trucks being piloted in 2026, such as Casella's work for Concord, NH, still have human drivers. Only the cart lifting is automated.
Municipal refuse truck driver jobs usually require a commercial driver's licence (CDL Class B) for the vehicle being operated, so the law expects a licensed human driver.

Agentic AI recruiting tools already handle sourcing, screening, outreach, scheduling and structured or conversational screening interviews end to end. Vendors still advise keeping a human in the loop for final hiring decisions.
Vendors say AI agents can run structured, role-specific interviews without live scheduling and can score candidates.

Gaming regulators license casino employees and key employees, including HR managers in Ohio. Licensing covers the hire's suitability, not who conducts the interview. The final hiring decision and the check that new hires are licensed are still done by accountable managers.

A 2025 survey of LLM-based scientific agents describes planner modules that break broad research aims into ordered steps (hypotheses, experiment design, analysis, validation), with replanning when results are uncertain. This is the detailed-planning sub-step that agents can draft end to end.

Project2Task (arXiv, August 2026) proposes graph-guided project-level planning that turns a project brief into candidate contributions and ordered tasks for autonomous research. This shows that turning broad goals into plans is a current agent capability, but it is research-stage work, not a proven replacement for a manager's judgement.

Commercial agents such as ClickUp's research roadmap planner break research goals into tasks with roles and deadlines. Setting the goals themselves within management's outline still requires organizational judgement, choices about resources, and agreement from stakeholders, and no licence or law requires a human to sign the plan.

Distributors such as Wurl already send each channel's schedule to Gracenote automatically. The feed covers tomorrow plus six days and includes episode IDs, titles, descriptions, original air dates and start times, so the step of passing schedule information to outlets is largely done by software today.

A patented EPG provisioning system takes broadcast traffic data, reformats it for each guide provider and sends it out in real time. This is a system design, not proof of a deployed product, but it shows that both the checking-and-formatting and the delivery sub-steps can be automated.

Clipsource says it can automate the distribution of linear and TV/VOD listings straight from planning sources. That covers the main sub-steps through software alone, with no physical presence needed. My one search found nothing saying a licensed human must sign off on listings, though I did not check this point directly.

Under CMS medical-direction rules, the anesthesiologist must personally do all seven required activities for each of 2 to 4 concurrent cases, including staying physically present and available for emergencies. Missing even one activity disqualifies the claim.

AI platforms such as Qventus, which connect to the EHR, automate operating-room scheduling. Vendors like ScheduleForward say they coordinate anesthesia coverage and rotations, though these claims come from the vendors and are unverified. These tools cover the planning and logistics part of coordinating staff.

Staffing software claims it can coordinate anesthesia coverage and fair rotations, but this is marketing. Directing nurses and technicians in real time during a case, at the bedside, remains a human job.

The Passport immobilization API works with tow processors such as AutoReturn. An officer can request a tow from a handheld device, get the fees calculated in real time, and follow the tow's status in a central back-end system. This means the arranging step is already digital and could be scripted by an agent.
Tow-dispatch software sends requests straight to drivers' phones in place of manual rotation, with automatic assignment and timestamps. The dispatch and rotation sub-steps can be automated.

Department policies require an officer to tag or sticker the vehicle on site, wait 24 to 72 hours, and re-check before towing. Some also require a consent form from the private property owner. This confirms that physical presence and the officer's legal authorization are needed for the parts an agent cannot do, such as verifying the vehicle and pointing the driver to it on scene.

Multnomah County's job profile says animal control officers examine animals to judge how severe a sickness or injury is, then arrange medical care and take the animal to a veterinarian. That means hands-on handling and transport in the field.

Long Beach's job classification says officers give routine care and preventive treatment under a veterinarian's direction. The officer does the triage, and a licensed vet decides on and provides the medical treatment.

The AI pet-health apps I found screen photos for skin, weight and wellness problems and send users to a vet. They say they are not diagnostic tools, and none of them does validated injury triage. So AI can help from photos, but it can't do the physical exam.

Several AI breed-matching tools, including PawMatch, which is built on Gemini, ask about the owner's lifestyle, living situation and preferences and score them against databases of about 170–195 breeds to recommend specific breeds. That covers the research and matching part of purchase advice.

Expert buying advice often means seeing the individual animal in person: watching how it is caught, led, groomed, tacked and tied, and spotting signs that it was worked beforehand to calm it down. An agent without a body can't do this.

Extension guidance recommends taking along a trainer who knows the buyer's riding level and goals. The buyer handles and rides the horse in person, and a vet exam follows. No licence is needed to give purchase advice; only the vet exam is a separate professional act.

Keno writer and runner jobs include scanning winning tickets, working out winnings, paying customers in cash and keeping a personal cash bank balanced. These steps are physical and need someone present at the window or on the floor.

The rule lets a human writer or a self-service kiosk redeem winning tickets once the sports wagering system has checked them. So checking tickets and working out payouts is already automated in fixed systems, not done by a general AI agent.
Sportsbooks have not widely adopted full self-service cash-out machines because of technical, regulatory and risk concerns. Mobile accounts pay winnings out digitally, so no paper ticket is needed.

Livestock AI tools like Betty and VetWiz suggest likely diseases from symptoms the farmer enters, and Betty can point farmers to a local vet. But the breeder still has to examine the animal, and none of these tools combines AI triage with direct vet telehealth for livestock.

State veterinary practice acts, such as Florida's, let owners and their regular employees treat their own animals. So a licence is not required for minor treatment, though diseases of public-health significance need a licensed vet.
California's owner exemption (B&P Code 4827) lets bona fide owners give veterinary care to their own animals, except for certain specified procedures.

Australia's national competency unit AHCAIS303 is assessed through observed workplace practice. It requires the inseminator to restrain the animal, thaw the semen and perform the insemination by hand, which an agent with no body cannot do.

In Tyrol, Austria, insemination technicians must hold a certificate based on veterinary or inseminator training and declare the activity to the Chamber of Agriculture. People without the certificate can be banned from practising.
UK equine guidance (BEVA) says AI technicians must complete an approved AI technician course before inseminating mares, so a trained human has to do the procedure.
A DOL-listed carpenter helper posting describes the work as physical: building wood forms so they are aligned and plumb, then helping lift them to the required height.
Helpers build rough wooden structures such as concrete forms, gang forms and column forms from sketches, blueprints or verbal instructions, with a carpenter directing the work.

Software such as Tekla Structures automates formwork layout and planning in BIM. That planning is done by engineers and foremen; the helper's own work of building and raising forms is hands-on and cannot be done through software.

HR case-management and AI-agent products (for example ServiceNow Now Assist and Newgen) handle grievance intake, documentation, case summaries and suggested resolutions. A human still validates the findings and resolves the case.

In a typical union grievance procedure, the first step is an informal meeting between the employee, a steward and the immediate supervisor to resolve the matter. The step depends on face-to-face discussion and negotiation.
Grievance steps carry contractual deadlines and require written management responses, which an AI can draft. The decisions belong to designated management representatives.

Under 10 CFR 50.54(i) and 55.3, only NRC-licensed operators or senior operators may manipulate controls that directly affect reactivity or power level. Licensed operators must be at the controls at all times (50.54(k)), and a person who directs another to manipulate the controls counts as manipulating them.

In July 2026, INL, UIUC and Purdue used a reinforcement-learning digital twin to remotely and autonomously move an auxiliary control rod on the low-power PUR-1 research reactor. This was an expert-supervised experiment with the reactor's own safety systems keeping the final say. It was not a general AI agent running a commercial power reactor.

Researchers describe the work as an early step toward letting AI eventually assist in reactor operation, which means autonomous control of commercial plant rods, flux and coolant temperature is not deployed in October 2026.

A patented load-confirmation tool runs the final load manifest accuracy check electronically, a check once done by hand. It starts when loading staff send a 'load complete' notification, so a human still triggers it from the floor.
Dock management systems spot deviations such as delays, documentation problems or busy docks and raise them as automatic alerts, so people only handle the exceptions.

In Infor WMS receiving, the system creates expected-load records and staff note discrepancies at the dock; EDI and RF devices remove most of the paper. Problems are still found physically and entered by people.

OT aides work under close supervision of a licensed OT or OTA. They only do delegated routine tasks: helping patients carry out the regimens the therapist sets, moving patients to and from the treatment area, and setting up, cleaning and storing equipment.
O*NET describes the occupation as hands-on patient support and equipment preparation inside therapy programs that a therapist directs.

2026 AI tools draft OT treatment plans, SOAP notes and home exercise programs, but their own marketing says the output is only a starting point that the clinician must review and edit. That helps with the planning paperwork, not with delivering in-person therapy.

O*NET lists directing kitchen operations, including the presentation and serving of food, as a task of private household cooks. Their main tasks are cooking, shopping and serving meals to the family and guests in the home.

The work involves standing for long periods, working at hot stoves, cleaning work areas, knife skills and hand-eye coordination. Similar cook postings add plating, garnishing and portion control, so the role depends on hands-on work in the kitchen.

AI kitchen tools such as Chefpilot, AIKA and KitchenCommand handle inventory, recipe generation, meal planning, scaling and shopping lists. These are planning and admin steps that an agent can speed up, but none of these tools runs the physical kitchen or serves food.
Smart restroom systems such as Gojo Onvation only monitor dispenser levels and traffic. They send alerts and track response times, and a human attendant still has to service the restroom.

CMMS software such as OxMaint creates cleaning work orders when usage passes a set threshold and sends them to the nearest attendant. This automates scheduling only, not the cleaning or restocking itself.
Patents for washroom maintenance systems describe sensors that report usage data to staff, who then do the physical maintenance.

Search results only covered robot vacuums, which have height-clearance limits (bodies about 97mm tall) and get stuck under furniture. None addressed dusting furniture, walls or machines, which takes hand and arm work. The rated agent has no body at all, so dusting has to be done in person.

Floor robots skip areas behind thresholds or furniture over about 2cm high and avoid narrow gaps. This shows that even physical cleaning robots can't do above-floor dusting, and a software-only agent can't do any of it.

An industry report says furniture specifications prevent robots from reaching 100% floor coverage, and that loose fibres and cables tangle them. This confirms the task depends on physical work. No law or licence requires a human to do the dusting.

Smart controllers such as Rachio can be put into standby and have their schedules switched off from an app. A contractor can also be given limited access to run zones remotely during a blowout. This means software can handle only the controller and scheduling parts of winterizing and spring start-up.

Winterizing means physical work on site: closing the backflow preventer's ball valves, connecting an air compressor downstream of the device and blowing out the lines. The utility recommends a qualified licensed contractor for the blowout method.
The local plumbing code requires a certified tester to test the backflow preventer each season when it is reinstalled at spring start-up.

Sabre offers agentic APIs and an MCP translator. A vendor integration says AI agents can read live reservation and itinerary data in Sabre and handle booking changes, cancellations and rebookings across air, hotel and car travel.

Amadeus's 2026 report with Microsoft describes agentic AI working on airline transactions. In one trial, an airline AI agent found a booking, understood a change request, offered new options, explained the fare difference and started payment. This is reported as vendor-adjacent coverage.
Computer-use agents such as OpenAI Operator check availability and make reservations on their own through web interfaces. They hand control to a human for login, payment or CAPTCHA steps.

Self-service bag drop is kiosk and conveyor hardware: the passenger scans a boarding pass, prints and attaches the tag, and puts the bag on the belt. Bulky bags still go to staffed counters, so the core work is physical and is automated by machines, not by software agents.

Under 49 CFR 1544.203, checked baggage must be received by an authorized representative of the aircraft operator and handled under the TSA-approved security program. The rules also cover firearm declarations and refusing bags when the passenger will not consent to a search.

Kiosks can match bags to boarding passes, and LAX trialled self-service bag check with optional biometrics. Weighing, tagging and handling odd-size or cargo items, and directing passengers to loading points, still need people or physical machines on site.

Julius AI is reported to choose suitable statistical methods (regression, clustering, ARIMA) on its own, write and run Python/R code in a sandbox, and explain the results. It also runs t-tests, chi-square, ANOVA and regression, though complex multi-stage custom analyses are beyond what it handles well.

An academic study found that ChatGPT's statistical test recommendations depend heavily on how the prompt is written. This means a human must still specify the study design and research question and check the choice.
A 2026 review of AI statistics tools warns that ChatGPT sometimes makes calculation errors on complex problems and that critical results need checking. This supports keeping a human review step.

Commercial log-scanning and computer-vision products exist. LoadMon 3D-scans log trucks to get volume and diameter, and Roboflow measures log diameters and length and calculates Scribner, Doyle or International 1/4 volume. Both depend on cameras or scanners mounted at the site, so a software-only agent cannot take the measurements itself.
LoadMon scans log or bulk-wood trucks with more than 70 million points per scan and calculates volume, diameter and load skew in under 2 minutes. This hardware is installed at the site.
In Idaho it is illegal to scale logs for commercial use without a state licence, which requires written and practical exams, or without working as an apprentice under a licensed scaler.

Vendor material describes unattended truck-scale systems that use RFID cards, licence-plate readers and automated gates to identify vehicles and drivers and record weighments without an operator. This covers the sub-steps of capturing weights and supplier identities.

Weighbridge software connects to weight indicators, RFID readers, ANPR cameras and barriers, and keeps an audit trail. Once a vehicle is recognised, a weighment can start without anyone keying it in, so an agent could log and reconcile records through software. The truck still has to be physically on the scale, and exceptions need handling.

Several US states require a licensed public weighmaster or deputy to issue certified weight tickets. In Arizona, for example, nobody may act as a public weighmaster without a state licence, which keeps a human accountable for certified weights.

Blast design software such as Strayos and Orica SHOTPlus/BlastIQ can produce pattern layouts and charge designs from drone survey and drilling data, and can calculate the charge needed for a desired outcome. That covers the calculation part of the task, but someone still has to collect the field data.
Orica's SHOTPlus does 3-D blast design and timing simulation to flag problem areas before firing. It works as a decision aid for the engineer or blaster.

OSHA Subpart U allows only authorized, qualified blasters (as defined in 1926.901) to use explosives. The blaster must make sure everyone is out of the blast area before firing and must inspect the area after the blast. This is personal, on-site responsibility that a licensed human holds.

Steel Genie by ALLPLAN, launched in April 2026, uses AI to read structural drawings. It picks out member sizes, lengths, weights and connection details, then produces quantities and a 3D model that can be exported to fabrication tools.

Ferra and LIFT (SketchDeck.ai) take PDF drawing sets, detect beams, columns, braces and trusses, and output bills of materials and tonnage. The output is meant for a human estimator to review, not for use without checking.

ConstruSteel builds cut lists, nesting and CNC files from model data, which automates the material-preparation step. It does not interpret drawings directly, so the work sequence still depends on a person who knows the shop.

AI layers on top of CO2-based demand-controlled ventilation can set CO2 limits matched to ASHRAE 62.1 ventilation rates for each space type, learn occupancy patterns and adjust ventilation automatically. These are vendor claims, not certified compliance.

ASHRAE 62.1 sets accuracy and calibration rules for the CO2 sensors used in DCV. Sensors that are inaccurate or badly placed can cause under-ventilation, so someone still has to place, check and calibrate the hardware on site.

In Maryland, licensed stationary engineers oversee boilers and machinery including air-conditioning equipment, and every license grade requires a state exam. NYC requires a licensed engineer who works in boiler and ventilating rooms.

Norfolk Southern's AI inspection portals use trackside cameras and deep-learning models, but only on trains moving past them. They do not cover stationary equipment, and experts in the operations center review what the AI flags.
Under 49 CFR 215.13, freight cars must get a pre-departure inspection by a person the railroad designates under 215.11, who must have shown the knowledge and ability to inspect cars.
Canada's rules require a 'qualified person' with the right knowledge, training and experience to do pre-departure inspections.

Petrosoft's CStoreOffice back-office software for convenience stores and gas stations forecasts demand from past sales and builds suggested orders. An operator reviews and approves them. This is vendor marketing and has not been independently checked.
Petrosoft says AI back-office tools can analyze sales data, predict demand, suggest orders and set prices based on competitors and demand. These are also vendor claims.

Industry writing says AI can adjust gas station prices in real time from market and competitor data. Unpacking, checking, labeling and shelving incoming goods is still physical work that a software-only agent cannot do.

Battery testing requires a person to clean the terminals by hand, attach the red and black clamps to the right posts, and rock them until they make solid contact. Each of these steps is physical manipulation.
A dedicated tester runs the test and interprets the result (good / charge and retest / replace). An AI agent would add little beyond looking up specs or explaining the reading.

The procedure involves hands-on safety controls: switching the engine and ignition off, working with ventilation, keeping sparks and metal tools away from the terminals, and not reversing the clamps. None of these can be done through software alone.

Commercial AI tools already maintain watchlists, run ongoing monitoring of art-market and art-press news, generate recurring reports and send alerts when a tracked artist moves. This covers the monitoring and reading sub-steps, though the claims come from vendor marketing.

Artprice News, launched in late 2025, pairs art-market databases with Perplexity AI real-time search to cover museum exhibitions, art fairs, institutional appointments and market news, so an agent can produce automated digests of art-world activity.

Galleries, fairs and museums offer online viewing rooms and 360-degree virtual tours, which give an agent partial digital access to exhibitions. Going to shows in person still needs a physical visit, and the artist has to take in the material personally to develop their own ideas.

Commercial exercise-management platforms, such as 4C Strategies Exercise Manager, use AI to generate realistic emergency and continuity scenarios and exercise reports. They base these on an organization's own plans, dependencies and risk profiles.

Innovation Labs' Scenario Builder uses AI to design, run and evaluate tabletop emergency-management exercises for authorities and organizations. This shows that scenario design and evaluation sub-steps can already be automated.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38 requires employers to keep a written emergency action plan. OSHA guidance recommends evacuation drills, with the employer choosing how often. No licensed signatory is required for drill plans, but site-specific details such as exits, assembly areas and coordination with responders still need a human to check them.

FHWA's interim approval describes automated flagger assistance devices (AFADs) as remote-controlled STOP/SLOW signs or signal-and-gate-arm units. A human flagger runs them, either at the work zone or from a central location. They are physical roadside hardware, not software an AI agent could operate on its own.

A Roads & Bridges item quotes the MUTCD: an AFAD shall be operated only by a flagger trained on it and must never be left unattended while in use. This came from a trade publication's quote, and I did not check it against the current MUTCD text myself.
Iowa DOT's AFAD specifications require trained staff on site who can switch to manual flagging if a device fails, so a human has to be physically present.

SiteRecon sells landscaping site-audit software with mobile scoring templates, geotagged photos and notes, automated alerts for poorly scored sites, and client audit reports. The person on site still does the inspecting; the software records and reports it.
OrangeQC offers groundskeeper inspection forms with photos, scores and GPS tags, including templates for turf, irrigation and tree inspections. A field user has to fill them in on site.

Jotform offers a landscape maintenance site-audit AI agent template that collects conditions and photos through a chat interface. It structures what a human reports and does not observe the site itself.

O*NET lists 'Provide workers with assistance in performing duties as necessary to meet deadlines' as a task for this occupation. The occupation's core role is directly overseeing and coordinating crews that do the landscaping or groundskeeping work.

Job postings for this supervisor role describe hands-on field duties: planting or maintaining vegetation by mulching, fertilizing, watering, mowing or pruning. That needs a physical body, which a software-only agent does not have.

Related tasks in the same occupation also involve physical help, such as directing or assisting workers who maintain or repair power tools and motorized equipment. No license or legal sign-off is needed to do this help.

Landscaping platforms such as LMN, Jobber and Aspire already digitize crew timesheets, GPS time tracking, job costing and scheduling records. That makes it feasible for an agent to compile and update records through the software. However, no vendor clearly offers end-to-end AI automation of record upkeep.

The source data comes from field work done by the applicator and crew. Federal rules require pesticide application records that list the product, EPA registration number, amount applied and treated site. A human has to supply or confirm these field facts, but filling in the record itself is documentation, not a licensed sign-off.

Commercial applicators must keep records of all applications, available for inspection for at least two years. States often set stricter deadlines, for example completing records within three business days. This is a structured, rule-based task that an agent can track and enforce.

The machines that clear sidewalk snow on their own, such as the SnowBot Pro, are robots with GPS navigation and brushes. The reference AI agent has no physical body, so it cannot do this work. Vendor claims about labor savings are unverified and some are dated.
Even consumer snow-clearing robots like Yarbo need a person to set them up on site, so physical presence is still required.

The search found no software or robots for pouring cement curbs or repairing sidewalks. These are hands-on construction work, and a software agent could help only with small side jobs like scheduling or ordering materials.

Attentive.ai Automeasure measures landscape maintenance, snow and paving sites from aerial imagery for estimates and bids. The vendor claims over 98% accuracy, and a headline announces a partnership with LMN, an estimating and job-costing platform (only the headline was seen).

SiteRecon's AI maps turf, planting beds and paved areas from aerial imagery for takeoffs and says it offers open APIs and works with common CRMs and estimating software. So the measuring and costing steps can run without a site visit, though crew productivity rates, local pricing and the final bid still need a supervisor's judgment and review.

Landscaping business systems like Aspire (a ServiceTitan company) and LMN hold the estimating, job-costing and budget data. An agent can track budgets only if it is given access to these company accounts.

Under 40 CFR Part 171, anyone who uses or supervises restricted-use pesticides must be a certified applicator. A noncertified worker may apply them only under the direct supervision of a certified applicator.

Herbicide spraying is being automated with drones and robots, not software agents. Spray drones are used on ditches and roadsides, but their performance depends heavily on flight height, speed and weather. That automation needs a robotic body, which the reference technology does not have.

Utility vegetation management is testing autonomous drone spraying as a replacement for labour-intensive manual work. The manual job itself is physical: lifting, pushing and swinging nozzles and hoses.

Vendors say their agentic intake tools read borrower documents like pay stubs and tax forms, extract and check the data, and push it into the loan origination system (LOS), CRM or internal databases. Exceptions go to a person.
Layerup says its intake agent takes in 1003 loan applications, extracts and indexes the documents, and verifies income and assets inside existing mortgage workflows.

UiPath's lending automation connects to major LOS platforms (Encompass, nCino, Empower) and works alongside them. Vesta, an AI-native LOS, says about 40% of tasks run on its platform are handled by AI agents, and issues needing human review are escalated. Both figures are the vendors' own claims.

Customers give utilities keys to reach meters, or leave them with a neighbor or on the premises. Meter readers keep and use these keys in the field, so a person has to physically find that a key is lost or broken before anything can be reported.

Utility procedures send access problems, including key or combination fixes, to case handling by customer contact staff and meter reading staff. That handling happens in internal systems, where an agent could write and file the report.
Field-service apps for utilities already record site-access blocks, such as a locked access door, as structured digital entries. This shows the reporting step can be done in software.

USPS Automated Package Verification (APV) checks parcel postage from scanned weight and dimensions. USPS still says detection is imperfect and that staff find many discrepancies by hand during acceptance and processing. Software handles postage calculation and checking, but a person or physical equipment has to capture the inputs.

Under Publication 52, acceptance staff must look closely at every side of each mailpiece for hazmat markings and old labels, and must ask the customer about hazardous contents. This is physical, face-to-face handling and inspection at the counter.

Retail guidance says associates must ask any follow-up questions needed to accept each package safely, and must reject it if the contents are unknown. Unclear cases go to the postmaster or the PCSC for a ruling.
Customers can already pick a PO box size and location, reserve it and pay for it online through USPS's reservation system. That covers the selection, application and payment sub-steps.
Renters must show two current forms of ID in person, one a photo ID and one proving their address, together with PS Form 1093 at the Post Office where the box is located.
A Post Office employee checks the IDs during business hours and then hands over the keys or the combination number. This step needs someone physically present.

Manufacturer glass configurators such as AGC's can configure single, insulating and laminated glazing and find products by optical, thermal, acoustic and safety performance. This is the part of the task that turns a specification into a glass type, and an agent can do it in software.
Vitro Construct, which is built on LBNL's WINDOW software, lets users choose pane count, thickness, coatings and laminates from tables. An agent operating a browser could run these tools.

Building codes such as IRC R308 set rules for safety glazing in hazardous locations and require permanent marks on the glass. These rules are written down and an agent can check them. No licence or sign-off by the glazier is required to select the glass. The physical work is still done by a person: picking the actual sheet or mirror from stock, checking its color by eye and matching existing glass on site.

KONE 24/7 Connected Services uses cloud-based AI analytics on sensor data to flag elevator and escalator faults and to judge whether each one is critical. Technicians get alerts and diagnoses before they reach the site. A human still confirms and fixes the fault on site, so the AI helps with fault-finding but does not do it.

Otis ONE sends equipment sensor data to the cloud so engineers can spot and diagnose faults before arriving on site. The physical checks of brakes, motors, switches and controllers with meters and other test equipment are still done by hand.
In Illinois, a person needs an elevator mechanic license to maintain, alter or repair a conveyance. This puts troubleshooting work on the equipment in the hands of licensed people.

AI-native test frameworks such as GlobalLogic TAK and HCLTech Turbo, along with LLM multi-agent systems like NeTestLLM, can generate, run and analyse validation tests for telecom equipment and protocols from software. This covers the remote, software-side checks of updated equipment.

Patent filings and products describe remote autonomous testing of telecom and wireless networks without a site visit. That supports delegating post-update functional checks, but on-site physical test hookups and visual observation still need a human.

Some states license low-voltage and telecom technicians. For example, Rhode Island's TST licence covers installing, servicing and testing systems. These licences govern who works on the equipment, but they generally do not require a licensed person to sign off on each test.

AMETEK Insight is a cloud tool that lets operators monitor battery performance, adjust charge settings and update charger firmware remotely. This covers the digital part of operating a charger, but not repairing one.

ACTview is a browser-based platform that collects data from Quantum chargers and BATTview battery monitors to help diagnose charger and battery problems. An agent could analyze this data, but a person still has to do the physical repair: replacing components, rewiring, connecting batteries.

Saft Intelli-Connect monitors temperature, current, voltage and electrolyte level remotely so maintenance can be scheduled by condition. This helps with diagnosis and planning, but the hands-on maintenance stays physical.

AI predictive-maintenance tools already use FFT-based vibration analysis from installed sensors to flag faults such as misalignment, unbalance, loose foot, bearing defects and worn belts. This covers only the monitoring and analysis part of the task, and it depends on sensors and data that are already in place.

Most of the task happens on the machine itself: watching and listening to it run and placing test leads on circuits. Using test instruments on energized equipment is limited to qualified persons wearing arc-flash PPE.

Vendor and practitioner sources say poor data is the most common reason AI diagnostics fail. A human still has to observe the machine and take the measurements, while the AI helps by interpreting readings and suggesting troubleshooting steps.

Modern CMMS platforms already support reorder points, safety stock calculations and automated purchase requests. AI adds dynamic reorder thresholds. The source is a vendor blog, so treat it as vendor-reported.

Technicians log the parts they use against a work order from a mobile device, which updates inventory. Purchase orders are created automatically when stock falls to its minimum. The ground truth about what was actually used still comes from the technician who did the repair. This is a vendor claim and has not been independently checked.
AI systems can pull parts lists into generated work orders and send them on for action. This is vendor marketing, so treat it as vendor-reported.
Setting up lathe work means physically clamping stock in a chuck, sometimes changing chucks, and loosening locking rings with a spanner. All of this is hands-on work with hand tools at the machine.

Shop procedures require the operator to physically check that the chuck is tight and the workpiece is rigidly secured, support long stock with a tailstock, and remove the chuck key before starting. The hazards include fingers caught by slipping jaws and long workpieces bending and striking the operator.

OSHA 1910.212 places machine-guarding duties on employers and says hand tools for loading may supplement guarding but not replace it. It does not require a licensed person to load the lathe, so the barrier here is physical rather than legal.

LevelField-1 is an open-source vision-language model that reads 2D drawings, pulls out dimensions and tolerances, and proposes process routes across 18 machining types. Its developer reports that process engineers still review the output and that drafting time fell by about 60% in pilots. These figures are the developer's own and have not been independently checked.
An academic pipeline for reading engineering drawings retrieved dimensions with about 81% end-to-end accuracy. That is good enough to speed up the work, but a human still has to check the results.

An informal test found that frontier language models can only sometimes plan how to machine simple parts. This suggests a human is still needed to confirm the operation sequence and the equipment choice.
O*NET lists marking identification numbers or symbols onto patterns or templates as a core task for metal and plastic patternmakers. The work is done by hand on physical patterns.

Foundries put numbers on patterns, using prefix letters for the intended metal (B for bronze, C for cast iron) and paint colours for features like machined surfaces. An agent could help pick or look up the right code, but someone has to apply it physically.

Pattern labels support process control and quality tracking, and foundries use equipment that embosses date codes and heat numbers onto patterns. The marking itself is physical, so software can only help with the codes and the label design.

Folding and stretching fabric edges while sewing is done by hand at the machine. The automated alternatives are specialised robot hardware such as F-FOLD end-effectors and dual-roller stretch systems, not software agents.

Robotic sewing uses grippers, suction devices and vision-guided hardware to hold and tension fabric. Many complex operations are still hard to automate cost-effectively, and a software agent with no body cannot do any of it.
Research on stretching fabric during automated sewing relies on physical roller mechanisms that match fabric tension to sewing speed, which confirms this is a manual or mechanical task.

Foundry ERP software such as iCast ERP lists pattern management features, including lifecycle tracking, maintenance schedules and history. An agent with computer use could enter, update and cross-reference these records in software like this.
FOMIS foundry software covers pattern and tool administration together with traceability and certificate records. This shows pattern record-keeping is already digitised in commercial systems.
