In general ERPs like Epicor, patterns are tracked as inventory items through standard transaction reports. That makes record upkeep a software job, but a human on the shop floor still has to check the physical pattern's condition, measurements, tags and storage location.

AI computer-vision and gas-monitoring tools for chemical plants flag unsafe conditions and suspend permits automatically. Vendors such as Intenseye present them as an addition to gas detection and process-safety instruments, not a replacement. This is support for the human operator.

Industry guidance (AIChE CCPS) calls for continuous monitoring on site, stopping work when combustible gas is found, and gas testing by certified testers. These are physical steps done in the field that only a qualified person can carry out.

Under OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119, employers must train process operators and run a hot work permit program. Training providers and site policies say permits must be approved and signed by authorized people, so a human stays accountable for the safety precautions.

One patented chain-wear monitor uses a proximity sensor and a camera mounted along the conveyor to measure chain pitch and estimate wear. This kind of tool needs dedicated hardware installed on the machine, so a software-only agent cannot do the inspection alone.

Vendors describe AI vision systems that flag belt tears, edge wear and splice wear and send alerts to maintenance software. These need fixed cameras on site. Without them, someone has to look at and handle the chains, belts or scrolls in person, and an agent could only help with interpreting images or keeping records.
Vendor pages claim AI vision cameras can detect belt tears and estimate remaining belt life, but the accuracy figures they give have not been checked independently.

O*NET lists 'Examine products to verify conformance to quality standards' as a core task of production helpers. It describes the role as hands-on, lower-skill work alongside loading machines, moving stock and packing goods.

Employer postings for production helpers combine watching for defects and checking finished goods for width and length with heavy lifting (up to 75 lbs) on the plant floor. The inspection is done in person by handling and measuring products.

AI visual inspection systems such as Siemens' end-of-line defect detection can automate defect checks, but they need cameras and sensors installed on the line. That is purpose-built hardware, not something a software-only agent can reach by default.

In the O*NET profile for Helpers--Production Workers (51-9198.00), the role is less-skilled support for production workers. Listed duties include loading and unloading machines and moving materials between storage and work areas. This is physical, on-site work that a software-only agent cannot do.
The ASU mirror of the O*NET profile describes the occupation as hands-on production support, with a median wage of $38,890 and a projected change of -2.8% from 2025 to 2035.

The task 'Prepare raw materials for processing' appears in O*NET task comparisons for production occupations. The work is handling materials: cutting, mixing, sorting and staging them. An agent could only help with a small slice, such as looking up specs or recipes.
Removing flash by hand still means cutting it off with a knife or hammer and finishing it with a scraper, which is physical, labor-intensive work.
When flash removal is automated, it is done by physical equipment such as cryogenic tumbling drums, not by software agents.
Robotic deflashing uses physical cutters that follow the part. That needs robotics, which the reference AI agents do not have.

Under 49 CFR Part 225, railroads must prepare accident/incident reports following the FRA Guide. When a railroad blames human factors, the employee can submit a personal supplement (Form FRA F 6180.78). That makes the engineer's own first-hand account and sign-off central to the report.

Software already structures and processes the formal reports. FRA's AIRGNET generates Part 225 accident/incident reports, and commercial tools such as PST's AIRS manage incident reporting. Neither supplies what the crew saw or heard.

Locomotive event recorders capture detailed operating data (speed, braking, signals) that could be used to reconstruct incidents. This data could feed a drafted report, but it sits inside railroad systems an outside agent would not normally reach.

Governments publish their grain and agricultural tariff-quota allocation rules openly and run them through online systems such as Switzerland's e-quota and India's e-TRQ, so an agent can read the rules and apply the formulas digitally.

Grain quota allocation rules are documented formulas, such as first come, first served or shares based on past export tonnage. An agent can compute them from records, but it needs the firm's own trade history and access to the government portal.

US farm-program base and quota calculations follow published formulas, and university spreadsheet tools exist to compute them. Official figures still come from FSA allocation summaries, so a human needs to check the results against those.

As of 2026, AI and ODR tools mainly help human mediators with intake, scheduling, analytics and drafting. Commentators say AI should complement rather than replace human judgment, and that it struggles with parties' emotions and the dynamics of negotiation.

Research such as 'Robots in the Middle' found that LLMs can understand dispute scenarios, recommend interventions and draft neutral messages. That makes them capable assistants for some sub-steps of facilitation.
Court-annexed mediator rosters require qualified, trained people. Requirements include 40 hours of training, co-mediation experience, and in some cases bar membership or a behavioral-science degree.

OSHA 1910.269 sets fall-protection and line-clearance trimmer rules, including a required safety saddle and a second qualified trimmer nearby in some conditions. These rules assume a qualified human worker is climbing the tree.

A 2022 FWPA review found the range of robotic tree-climbing and pruning equipment very limited. Systems like the Patas still have problems with weight and agility, and UAV options need more development before they are usable. In any case these are robots, outside the software-only reference technology.
OSHA interpretation on safety saddles and body belts for line-clearance tree trimmers who climb, under 1910.269(g) and (r)(8).

OSHA's wood chipper bulletin describes operators feeding limbs into chippers by hand, which puts them right next to the infeed rollers and knives. It covers training and safe work practices, and it reports a fatal case where an operator was pulled into the machine.
ANSI Z133.1 requires quick-stop and reverse controls on the infeed that are within easy reach of the worker feeding the chipper. That assumes a person is physically at the machine running it.

WorkSafe NZ guidance says chipper operators must be trained and competent and should be protected from the infeed rollers by guarding and stop devices. The task is physical machine handling and has no digital part an AI agent could do.

Job postings describe this work as picking up and carrying limbs, logs and debris by hand, feeding wood into chippers and running stump grinders. All of it is on-site physical work, so a software-only agent cannot do it.
Workers must regularly lift up to 50 lbs to load and unload equipment, and bend, walk, stand and stoop for long periods outdoors in extreme weather.

ANSI Z133 tree care safety rules, which state regulation adopts, cover on-site work such as tree removal, chipping, keeping clear of the work zone and using equipment. This is hazard management in the field rather than a sign-off that only a human can give.
Deep root fertilization is hands-on field work. Workers drill or air-spade a grid of holes in the root zone and inject liquid fertilizer into them. A software-only agent cannot do this.
Applying fertilizer alone usually needs no licence. A licence is required when the product contains a pesticide, so licensing is not the main barrier for this task.

Connecticut's arborist licence covers feeding and fertilizing trees and tests tree nutrition and how to diagnose deficiencies. AI could help with this knowledge, but a person still has to apply the treatment physically.

AI agent skills and generators already draft performance improvement plans and disciplinary documents end to end from employee context and policy. Vendors say these tools do not verify facts or make the final decision, so HR keeps review and final edits.
A free AI PIP draft generator released in May 2026 produces structured drafts with goals and check-in schedules, and HR stays in control of final edits.

Employers remain liable for discriminatory outcomes from automated HR tools, even when a vendor promises compliance. This makes meaningful human review of adverse employment decisions necessary in practice.

Ramp's Agents for AP (launched October 2025) code, route for approval and process invoice payments in its Bill Pay product. Ramp says this is close to full automation, but that is the vendor's own claim, and humans usually still approve payments.
Tour leaders often collect local payments in cash at the start of a tour and pay for services with it during the trip. That on-site cash handling needs a person there.

Group leaders are expected to keep detailed logs of what they spend (date, who was paid, amount, purpose) and to reconcile them with receipts. An agent can keep this record digitally, but it works from receipts and inputs a human provides.

O*NET says Passenger Attendants (bus aides, bus monitors, transportation aides) work in person to keep passengers safe on ships, buses and trains and in stations and terminals. Their duties include answering questions, requests and complaints and giving route and timetable information.

Vendors say AI chatbots for airlines and rail already answer travel questions, take complaints and rebook trips, with claimed autonomous resolution rates of about 48% to 80%. These figures come from the vendors themselves, and the tools work through digital channels, not on board the vehicle.
Ada's own 2026 research found that only 24% of consumers said AI fully resolved their issue without a human, so harder requests and complaints still go to people.

AI roleplay and coaching platforms such as FullyRamped and PitchMonster already run practice product demos with simulated buyers. They give automated feedback and push product knowledge to keep messaging consistent. That covers the scripting, practice and feedback parts of training.

Demonstrator work involves physical tasks like preparing and serving samples, using small appliances and keeping the station clean. Training for it therefore includes hands-on, in-person instruction that an agent cannot do.

Food-safety certification for demonstrators (provincial certificates, Costco's own test) is something the demonstrators themselves must hold. The person training them does not need a licence, so no rule says a human must deliver the training.

AI coaching apps released in 2026, such as NutriTracker, FitQoach and AllTrain, write meal plans and workout programs, track macros and adjust targets, but the user still has to eat, exercise and sleep in person. These are self-reported store listings.

Trainer platforms such as ABC Trainerize add AI workout builders and meal planners, link to wearables, and can produce a full 7-day meal plan with a grocery list in minutes. This covers only the planning and tracking part of the routine. The second source is a vendor blog.

A vendor guide on AI for personal trainers advises keeping a human's clinical judgment in the loop. Following a diet, sleep and exercise routine is bodily work only the model can do, and no law or license is involved.
Cloud fleet tools such as UTAX Fleetmanager watch device status across a fleet, alert staff when a fault appears and update firmware remotely. This lets software take over part of the monitoring.

Epson Remote Services sends alerts and lets staff reboot devices and clean printheads remotely. Its stated purpose is to make field visits more efficient, which means hands-on visits are still needed.

PRISMA production-printer monitoring alerts operators when they need to act, for example to load media or add consumables. Many adjustments, like clearing jams, loading media and aligning feeds, have to be done by hand at the machine.

Deere's autonomous tractor app lets a farmer set implement width, speed, turn speed and tillage depth, and start or stop the machine remotely. This was shown at CES 2024 in a beta for specialized hardware, not general-purpose AI agents. The mechanisms on most machinery are still set by hand at the machine.

Cal/OSHA requires an operator stationed at the controls of a moving agricultural tractor. Driverless operation has only an experimental variance, and the staff recommended denying a petition to make it general.

Under federal OSHA (29 CFR 1928), operators must wear seat belts on tractors with ROPS and must receive safety instruction when first assigned and at least once a year. This assumes a human operator is physically present.

Farm autonomy as of 2026, such as PTx Trimble OutRun, automates tractor-pulled grain carts in the field. An operator is still needed to unload into the truck, and the truck haul itself is still done by a human driver. In any case this is robotic hardware, not a software-only agent.

Driving a vehicle on public roads needs a physically present driver. Even under the MAP-21 farm CDL exemption, the farm truck driver must hold a valid licence (noncommercial at minimum), and a CDL is required beyond 150 air miles or for hazmat.
Covered farm vehicle rules are tied to the driver: there are age minimums, combination vehicles require a medical certificate, and a designation form must be carried in the cab.

Feed-management software such as TMR Tracker builds rations in desktop software and sends the instructions to the mixer's scale indicator. The indicator shows a target weight for each ingredient, but a person still has to load the ingredients physically. Software can only help with calculating amounts and keeping records.

In Agrimatics' loading workflow, the operator starts a batch and adds each ingredient by hand while load cells track the weight. The system can recalculate the remaining ingredient amounts, but it cannot do the mixing.

FDA rules allow drugs to be mixed into feed only at approved levels. Medicated feed under the Veterinary Feed Directive needs a veterinarian's written order, but a farmworker can do the mixing on the farm without a licence when that order exists. The legal responsibility belongs to the veterinarian and the producer, so it does not require a human to do the mixing.

Under OSHA's logging rules, a back cut must be made in every tree being felled. It has to leave enough hinge wood to hold the tree to the stump for most of its fall so the tree falls in the intended direction. This is hands-on chainsaw work at the stump.

Errors in back-cut depth or height make the hinge fail, cause kickback or lead to inaccurate falls. NIOSH FACE investigations link these errors to logger deaths. Doing the cut correctly depends on real-time physical judgment and handling the saw.
The OSHA and state safety procedures for felling with a chainsaw regulate how the cut is done. They do not require any licence sign-off, so the main barrier is physical, not legal.
O*NET lists 'Trim off the tops and limbs of trees, using chainsaws, delimbers, or axes' as a core faller task. It is hands-on work with chainsaws, delimbers or axes at the felling site.

NIOSH reports describe deadly physical hazards in this work, such as a timber faller killed by a hung limb, and recommend following OSHA logging-standard chainsaw procedures. This confirms the task needs a person on site.

OSHA cited a logging company because an employee was limbing trees with a chainsaw without face protection. Limbing is done by hand with a chainsaw in the forest, outside any software system an AI agent can operate.

Automating log loading with machine control (reinforcement learning on a simulated forwarder crane) is still at the research-prototype stage. It requires robotic or hydraulic actuation, which a software-only AI agent does not have.

Remote operation of stationary knuckleboom loaders works through electric-over-hydraulic joysticks controlled by a human operator. It is physical machinery, not software an agent could normally reach.
Truck-mounted crane makers like Hiab offer only semi-automatic functions such as automatic folding. Full automation is still being developed through partnerships like the one with Forterra.

In aggregate surfacing, workers embed roofing gravel into one or two pour coats of hot asphalt at set rates (for example 3.0 kg/m2 of asphalt with 20 kg/m2 of gravel). The asphalt must cover the felts with no skips, and the gravel must cover the asphalt with no gaps. This is manual work done on the roof itself.
Manufacturer instructions describe single-pour and double-pour flood coat and gravel application as hands-on installation steps done with hot bitumen on site.
Built-up roofing is finished with a last flood coat that has gravel or granules embedded in it. The work is done on site and the surfacing step can take several hours.
Painter helper job postings list cleaning brushes and spray guns and keeping the work area clean among the essential manual duties.
Helpers operate, clean and maintain painting equipment such as sprayers, pumps and pressure washers. This is hands-on work that a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do.
Hawaii's state class specification calls painter helper duties routine, repetitive, manual and semi-skilled, and the role is entry level.

The machines that already automate sanding before painting are force-controlled industrial robots and cobots, which are physical hardware, not software agents. The reference AI agent has no body or robotics.
Sanding and buffing to prepare a surface for paint means applying the right pressure to the actual surface, swapping abrasive discs and controlling dust. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.

Even a dedicated aerospace sanding robot project still needed people for most of the work: the robot was grinding for only 8% of total processing time. Software can help at most with things like choosing abrasives or explaining the procedure.
The rail is cut with a hand-held hydraulic abrasive saw that an operator places on the rail and pivots to cut from either side. This is physical work done on the track.
Competency standards require cutting rail safely and accurately to procedure. That depends on hands-on knowledge: identifying rail by roll marks, defect length and depth limits, and pre-heating.
A rail-cutting incident investigation stressed on-site risk control and physical checks of the clearance gauge and the cut rails before the track goes back into service.
Spike pullers are either hand-operated hydraulic tools or self-propelled machines run by an operator from a cab on the track, so the work has to be done in person.
Handheld hydraulic spike pullers such as the Stanley SPL31 deliver about 16,647 lbs of pulling force and kick back at the operator, so a person has to hold and handle the tool.

Patents show spike-puller jaws worked by hydraulic cylinders, with a mechanical tie finder that locates ties as the machine runs. The work is mechanical and done on the track, with no software step an AI agent could take over.

Tie adzing means hands-on operation of a heavy machine on the track. The operator raises and lowers the cutterhead to offset the machine bouncing over uneven ties so the surface comes out smooth. An AI agent with no body or robotics cannot do this.
A 1937 archive photo shows railroad workers running Nordberg adzing machines to shave tie tops so tie plates can be fastened, which confirms the task is physical and done on the track itself.

Under FRA rules (49 CFR 214.341/214.355), roadway workers who run roadway maintenance machines must be trained and qualified by showing they can operate each machine safely in person, so the regulations require a qualified human operator.

AI repair assistants such as iFixit's FixBot only give diagnostic advice. A hands-on review found it gave generic guidance on a TV repair that would not power on, while the human still does all the physical work.

Connecticut licenses television, radio and electronics technicians and service dealers. This is a licence for the business and worker in a few states, not a sign-off required on each repair, and most jurisdictions have no such rule.
California requires businesses that repair electronics such as TVs, radios and stereos to register with the state, but it does not require a licensed human to sign each job.

Vending telemetry platforms such as Nayax AMIT 3.0 monitor machines in real time, send alerts and allow remote device control. They read data through DEX/GSM, so an agent can check fault codes and machine status from a distance.

Remote monitoring software alerts operators when a machine is down or out of order and can reset errors remotely. It flags faults but does not physically test coin acceptance, product dispensing or game mechanisms.
DEX-port telemetry sends audit data to cloud reporting at set intervals. Checking that the machine really works still needs someone on site to insert coins, make test vends and watch the mechanisms.

Under AWS D17.1, aerospace welders must hold performance qualification for their specific process, material, thickness, position and weld type. This includes tube-weld tests for tubes of 1 inch OD or smaller and eye exams. Customers commonly require this qualification by contract, so a human welder has to do the work.

IPC/WHMA-A-620 covers hand soldering and crimping of cable and harness work. Operator and inspector credentials, and the NASA-aligned Space training, include hands-on practical exams. That shows the task is manual work done by a human.

The task means handling tack welders, induction brazing chambers and soldering tools on physical parts. A software-only agent has no body, so the most it can do is look up weld procedures or parameters, which is a small part of the working time.

O*NET lists 'file, lap, and buff parts to fit, using hand and power tools' as a task for Electromechanical Equipment Assemblers (51-2023.00). It is hands-on material removal and finishing on physical parts.

The same hand-finishing task is listed for Hand Grinding and Polishing Workers (51-9022.00). That makes it a manual shop-floor activity that only robotics could do, and a software-only agent has no robotics.
Descriptions of the role show assemblers filing, lapping and buffing parts by hand with hand and power tools as part of physical assembly work.

O*NET lists using covering cloths so that equipment does not damage delicate fabrics as a core task for Pressers, Textile, Garment, and Related Materials (51-6021.00). The occupation operates steam and hydraulic pressing machines.
A press cloth is a thin cotton, muslin or organza layer placed by hand between the iron or press and the garment to prevent scorching, shine or melting, so the task is entirely physical manipulation.

Press cloths are physical products, such as the Dritz 594 silk organza cloth, which is dampened and laid over the fabric. Software has no role in performing the task, though an agent could at most look up fabric-care guidance.
Vendor listings describe automatic shoe-upper cutters whose nesting software and defect-detecting camera plan the cutting path. The leather is still loaded and cut by dedicated CNC hardware.

Leather cutting systems such as Elitron Kudos use automatic nesting software (EliNest, NesCUT). This automates the layout planning, but the cutting itself is done by a machine, not by a software agent.

An EU project built a lay-planning system for shoe-upper parts that can feed manual or numerically controlled cutters. So software helps with planning, and a person or a machine still does the physical cutting.

ShadeBar Pro is an inline system that uses a spectrophotometer to measure L*a*b* values on moving fabric and calculate Delta E colour differences in real time. That covers the colour-measurement step, but it needs dedicated sensor hardware on the line.

AI vision camera systems detect fabric defects and shade variation, but they need controlled lighting and cameras installed on the line. A software-only agent can analyse the data these systems produce, but it cannot examine or feel the cloth itself.

Vision-based colour inspection reports Delta E and CIELAB colour-difference data, which an agent could read against standards. Judging tactile qualities such as hand and texture still requires a person handling the fabric.

O*NET lists 'Follow blueprints to produce specific designs' as a Furniture Finishers task. The occupation's core work is hands-on with the wood: sanding, stripping old finishes, repairing surfaces, and applying stain, lacquer or wax.

A Canadian furniture finisher job posting lists reading blueprints and drawings as one duty within physical finishing work in a shop. An AI could help interpret the drawings, but a person has to do the finishing.
The other Furniture Finishers tasks on O*NET include masking areas, removing accessories and repairing cracks and dents. Each needs physical handling, and an agent without a body cannot do any of it.

A search for automated reupholstery turned up only low-quality, copied pages from unreliable sites. They describe robotic upholstery in high-volume factory production, not stripping and re-covering existing pieces. No credible source showed software-only agents doing this work. A body-less AI agent could at most give marginal help, such as looking up fabric, adhesive or solvent specs or drafting cut templates.

The task is hands-on work on the object itself: removing old covering, cutting and fitting fabric, tacking or gluing it down, and applying softeners, solvents, stains or polish. It requires being there in person, and no law or licence requires a human to sign off on it.

Inline analyzers paired with PLCs (BFI DynAcid, SensoTech LiquiSonic) can measure acid and iron-salt levels in pickling baths and dose acid automatically. That is dedicated plant automation, though, not something a software agent does through screens and documents. Where no such system is installed, an agent can only work out the dose amounts or log them.

In patented strip-cleaning line control, conductivity probes and an online titrator feed a PLC that adjusts acid and water additions. So the measure-and-dose loop is handled by plant hardware, not an AI agent.

OSHA rule 29 CFR 1910.94(d)(9) requires employees working around open-surface pickling tanks to be trained in hazards, protective equipment and first aid. The work involves handling corrosive chemicals in person, but no licence or human signature is required.

Launching a lifeboat is hands-on work done on deck and inside the boat: removing harbour pins, releasing gripes, working the winch brake, pulling the safety pin and working the hook-release lever, then steering the boat clear under engine. An agent with no body can't do any of this.

SOLAS Reg. III/3.2 requires survival craft to be handled by 'certified persons', meaning people who hold an STCW VI/2 Certificate of Proficiency in Survival Craft and Rescue Boats. The company and the master must make sure the crew assigned to these duties hold that certificate.

The STCW A-VI/2-1 competence trains a person to launch a survival craft or rescue boat and take charge of it in an emergency. This is a crew role in person, with a certificate that must be renewed every five years.
By 2026, AI agents can find, compare and buy products from a stated goal. Checkout support is still patchy: few merchants are live on in-chat checkout, and some large retailers block agents.
Professional suppliers of special-effects makeup, wigs and hair, such as The Costumer and Banbury Postiche, take orders online, so an agent could do the sourcing and ordering.
Custom wigs and hairpieces need precise head measurements and usually can't be returned. A person has to take the measurements, match colors on the performer, and check the goods when they arrive.

ScreenSkills' AI guidance for hair and make-up designers says AI can generate hair and makeup concepts from character descriptions, a script or historical references and act as a visual sounding board. It also says interpreting character nuance remains a human skill.
Diffusion models can change facial attributes and cosmetic styles, including makeup for a period-drama setting, and are trained on large datasets of historical clothing and character designs.

Concept sketching, reference research and digital character mockups are listed as higher-risk tasks for automation. Prosthetic sculpting and hands-on application stay lower risk. Making physical models therefore still needs a person, and a designer has to check historical accuracy and the result for each actor.
Job postings say roofer helpers help experienced roofers tear off or remove existing shingles and other roofing materials, then clean the roof deck to prepare for installation.
The work requires climbing ladders, working at heights with fall protection, using hand tools, and lifting 50 to 80 lbs. This is manual work that an agent without a body cannot do.
Helpers remove old roofing materials under the supervision of skilled roofers on the job site. The task is done entirely by hand on the roof, with no part of it done in software.

NFPA 1583 sets up mandatory fire-department fitness programs with an assessment at least once a year of aerobic capacity, strength, endurance, body composition and flexibility. The firefighter has to do the exercise in person, so it can't be delegated.

AI fitness apps can write workout plans and adjust them over time. That only touches planning, a small part of the work. The person still does all of the training. No firefighter-specific AI training tools turned up.
Exercise only improves the fitness of the person doing it. An agent with no body can't do any substantial part of the task.
D.A.R.E. sends specially trained, certified police officers into schools to teach the curriculum in person. Instructors must complete an 80-hour training course, and lessons run weekly in classrooms.
Local police departments run these as officer-led classroom programs that finish with a culmination ceremony. The officer's own presence and relationship with the students is the core of the program.

AI lesson-plan generators such as MagicSchool and Eduaide can draft lessons, activities and assessments, but sources say a human must review the drafts. Locally specific curricula need more rework. This supports the prep work only, not the in-person delivery.

InMoment's entertainment and recreation product collects feedback from surveys, social reviews and calls. It uses AI sentiment analysis to pull out themes so teams can act on them, which covers the analysis sub-steps of this task end to end.

Arch Amenities Group uses InMoment's XI Platform and its AI hub to collect and analyze survey and review feedback from gym and spa visits. The goal is location-level insight for improving the customer experience, which shows feedback-to-insight work already being delegated in recreation facilities.

TrustYou uses AI on surveys and reviews from across the web to improve service quality and to help respond to all feedback. Putting the changes into practice with staff and on-site operations is still the supervisor's job.

Arterial embalming is done by hand. The worker places the cannula and drainage, injects and massages the fluid, aspirates the cavities, sutures the incisions and disinfects the body. An agent with no body or robotics cannot do any of this.
The full process uses arterial, cavity, hypodermic and surface embalming. All of these are hands-on work on the body, followed by dressing and cosmetic preparation.
US states license embalmers, with requirements such as accredited mortuary-science training and an apprenticeship (Oregon example). This makes embalming a licensed professional activity.

Vendor AP agents already take in invoices, run OCR and line-item extraction, check the data and post it to an ERP, either as a draft for review or with no human touch. This is the same mechanism needed to post a sales slip to a customer's account.

Agent platforms advertised on AWS Marketplace cover the whole chain from intake and OCR through checking to ERP posting. Vendors claim 80–90% of items pass straight through without manual handling, but these figures are not independently verified.

AR agents check extracted billing data and act on it, for example by filling in ERP billing records. If the slips are paper, someone still has to scan them and file the physical copies, which is a hands-on step.

Ace Aquatec's A-BIOMASS uses AI with underwater cameras to measure salmon size and track growth in real time. Its A-HARVESTCAM estimates weight, weight distribution and quality on harvest lines. These need dedicated hardware installed at the site.

Roboflow's vision AI counts fish, estimates their length and weight, and detects sea lice, lesions and fin damage from stereo and mono cameras on an edge device, then sends results to farm systems through an API. An agent could analyze this output, but only where cameras are already installed.

Fraunhofer's image-based monitoring picks out individual fish in dense schools and measures their length and volume in tanks and net pens. It needs underwater cameras in place. Without them, a person has to observe the fish, beds and ponds in person.

Trimble CFHarvest is web and mobile software that sends work instructions, schedules and resource updates to harvesting crews' devices. An agent could draft and send this kind of written, scheduled communication.

Remsoft Operations, used at Forico, offers drag-and-drop crew scheduling. Forico reports it cut scheduling time by about 50%, a figure that comes from the vendor. This shows plan and schedule communication is already largely digital.

NZQA standards for crew foremen say the operational plan should be passed to the crew at a pre-start meeting on site. WorkSafe NZ also reviews daily tailgate meetings. This in-person part needs a human on site.

Farm platforms such as QuickBooks, Xero and farm-specific suites are becoming more autonomous. Tend sells one AI-driven platform for crop planning, sales, accounting and inventory, so agents can carry out accounting and sales sub-steps end to end.

Farm Focus put an AI agent ('Daisy', built on Salesforce Agentforce) into service for about 10,000 farm customers, covering CRM and marketing workflows. This shows marketing and customer management can be delegated in part.

H-2A job orders show that personnel work for farm supervisors is done in person: directing crews, giving warnings and discipline, safety training, and transport that needs a Farm Labor Contractor license. Employers must take responsibility for licensing and compliance, so this part depends on human trust and a person who signs.

Farm timekeeping software already handles the crew-level time data. Croptracker's Punch Clock groups workers into crews with crew leaders and produces pay and cost reports by crew, person or activity. Its records are also used for performance reviews, but the reviews themselves are rule-based and no AI agent writes them.

Farm payroll services such as OnPay and Netchex already process payroll for W-2, 1099 and H-2A agricultural workers, so an agent can compile and run the payroll reports. Evaluations, discipline and hiring decisions still depend on what the supervisor saw in the field, and a human has to review and approve them.

H-2A employers must keep records of each worker's earnings, hours offered and worked, and work locations for 3 years. The rule is about keeping the records, not about who prepares them. Secondary sources describe this rule, and it does not explicitly require a human to prepare or sign the reports.

Farm safety SaaS (Safe Ag Systems) digitizes the paperwork side of this task: training records with expiry alerts, risk assessments, incident reporting and compliance audits. Spotting hazards in the field and fixing them is still left to human supervisors.

AI camera safety monitoring (e.g., OpenBlue Worker Safety Advisor) runs on existing CCTV and is aimed at industrial, oil and gas, and construction sites, not open fields, forests or boats. Agricultural options such as AirAgri cover mainly lone-worker IoT alerts.

Under the Worker Protection Standard, agricultural employers must instruct supervisors on which protection duties they are responsible for. OSHA's field sanitation rule and General Duty Clause put responsibility for on-site compliance on the employer and the supervisor.
Fruit-picking robots such as Fieldwork Robotics' raspberry harvester are still on commercial-farm trials. Fleets are only expected from 2027, and they are physical robots, not software agents.
Commercial robotic harvesting is only now moving from pilots into early scaling, mostly in berries and apples. Hand harvesting is still a physical field job.
Washington's tree-fruit industry expected it to take 5 to 10 years before growers could hire a robotic apple harvester. This is an older source, so the timeline may be out of date.
Pelts are stretched and dried by hand on wire frames or wooden boards. They have to be centered and held under light tension, with pins, tacks or the stretcher's arms, all done physically.
Preparing a pelt involves skinning, turning it fur-side in or out depending on the species, tacking the legs and lips, and stuffing the paws. All of these are manual knife and hand steps.
The only automated stretching is done by industrial pelt-board machines for farmed mink, which are robots, not software agents. Trappers stretch pelts by hand.

Camera and machine-learning systems that measure fish length on board (iObserver, CatchMeter, NOAA's camera chute, UMass discard chute, CatchCam) are mostly research or pilot monitoring tools. They measure fish only after a human or a conveyor has handled them. None of them removes catch from fishing gear, which a software-only agent cannot do anyway.
Measuring fish and estimating their size from images on board needs dedicated chutes or conveyors with cameras: physical equipment that a general AI agent would not normally have access to.

Size rules require undersize fish or crustaceans to be released immediately and, as far as possible, alive. That is physical work done at the gear while it is being hauled. The law sets what must happen to the fish but does not require a licensed human to do the measuring.
Alaska's seafood harvesting career guide lists attaching nets, slings, hooks and other lifting devices to cables, booms and hoists as a hands-on deckhand duty on fishing vessels.

A U.S. Department of Labor seasonal job posting describes deckhands attaching nets, slings, hooks, blades or lifting devices to cables, booms, hoists or dredges. This is physical rigging work done on deck.

A Department of Labor shrimp and oyster vessel posting describes attaching and detaching apparatus devices to cable, boom, hoists, lines and nets. The work is manual and done on board, and software-only agents cannot do it.

AI fishing tools such as Catchwise combine catch history, AIS and ocean conditions to suggest where to fish, and are presented as supporting the skipper's judgment rather than replacing it. Its reported 6% efficiency gain across 3,800 trips comes from the company's own analysis.

ILO Convention C125 says fishing vessels it covers must carry a certificated skipper on board. National rules, such as Denmark's, set certificate-of-competency requirements for the master and the mate.

AI sonar products such as Kongsberg's SYAI on Simrad sonars detect fish, predict their movement and log detections. They are decision aids that run the equipment the crew uses. They do not direct the crew themselves.

Straightening a bent ring is hands-on work: the jeweler bends it gradually with pliers, a mandrel or a ring stretcher, protects the stones and polishes off tool marks. A software-only agent cannot do any of this. Caveat: this source is a low-quality, auto-generated how-to page and is used only to show the steps involved.

Harder metals such as platinum and titanium need more force or special heating equipment. Badly damaged pieces may need cutting and soldering, which is skilled bench work done by touch. Same caveat: low-quality source.

Pencil, a parametric CAD platform for jewelry, has released an AI jewelry CAD design agent. It produces rendered, parametric CAD designs meant for printing and casting, so the digital model-design sub-step can be delegated.

One vendor's AI text- or image-to-3D workflow exports STL files for 3D printing and investment casting. Its own guidance says a human still has to review stone settings and wall thickness before production, so the output needs checking.

RhinoArtisan 7.0 includes a Generative AI Studio that makes images and organic 3D models from text prompts. Physical fabrication (molds, printed or carved models, machine accessories, modified hand tools) still needs hands-on bench work.

Vendor material for 2026 says AI recruiting agents can source candidates, screen them against set criteria, send outreach and book interviews on their own. This covers most of the administrative recruiting work. These are vendor claims and I did not check them independently.

The EU AI Act classes AI used for recruitment, screening and candidate evaluation as high-risk and requires human oversight. A human therefore keeps responsibility for the hiring decision. Sources disagree on when this applies: one says enforcement starts 2 August 2026, while later ones say the Digital Omnibus moved it to 2 December 2027.

NYC Local Law 144 requires an independent bias audit and candidate notice for automated tools that substantially assist or replace hiring decisions. This limits how far hiring can be handed to AI without people in charge. The sources found did not say whether a human must make the final hiring decision.

In shuttle telematics systems, each vehicle's GPS unit reports when it enters or leaves stop and route geofences, and the server stores this as historical route and travel-time data. Route recording can therefore run with no manual entry.
Automatic logbook apps record each trip's start and end address, kilometres, date and start and end times, and sort trips by purpose. An agent could compile and format these records into route logs.

Commercial shuttle fleet platforms provide GPS tracking, schedule adherence monitoring and reporting exports. An agent needs access to these systems, and drivers must still note exceptions and detours the system misses and confirm the logs, so a human remains in the loop.

In the US, FRA treats remote-control locomotive operators as locomotive engineers under 49 CFR Part 240. They need certification, including a skills test, and must keep line of sight to the equipment or work inside a zone where only one remote-control locomotive operates.

Fully automated yard locomotives are still prototypes. DB Cargo and Bosch trialled one at Munich North, expect regulatory approval at the end of 2027 and plan to deploy it from 2028. These are purpose-built onboard systems, not general software agents.
Under FRA guidance, anyone who moves a locomotive must hold certification. The only exceptions are moves inside a repair area and moves under 100 feet for inspection.
Autonomous or remote-controlled aircraft tugs are still at the demonstration stage (a university prototype at Provo Airport). They are dedicated robotic vehicles, not software-only AI agents.
A semi-autonomous tug at JFK still needs federal approval, so a human tug operator remains the norm under aviation regulation.
Semi-autonomous towing is expected to arrive first in controlled areas such as hangars and closed ramp zones. Fully autonomous tugs are seen as some way off for busy airport operations.

Automated piece-picking from bins is done by physical robot systems (for example Bastian SmartPick with machine vision and a six-axis arm), not by software-only AI agents. The reference agent has no body, so it cannot do this.
In 2026 warehouse picking still mixes robots with humans who handle items by hand. Software only guides pickers and verifies picks; it does not do the picking.
Order-picking automation relies on hardware such as mobile robots, goods-to-person systems and robotic piece pickers, so the task is mainly physical manipulation.
Retail pricing software already works out an item's current price from its regular price (cost plus markup), sale and advertised prices, and competitor prices.
Automated markdown systems work out item prices from markdown profiles and updated sales data without a person doing the math.
AI markdown tools work out prices and send them to point-of-sale systems and electronic shelf labels, so the price calculation itself is digital.

To find an excavation point, a worker puts a camera or sonde into the pipe, sweeps the ground with a receiver, and marks the spot using a measuring wheel. All of these steps are physical work done on site.

In some states, excavators must physically mark the dig area with white paint, flags or stakes before requesting a utility locate. Arizona's new rule says electronic mapping alone does not meet this requirement.

Washington, Oregon and Iowa all require white-lining (marking the dig area in white) before calling 811, so marking is a physical field act. These sources do not require a licensed person to sign the marking.

State boards require the PTA to complete continuing education hours personally to renew a licence. Examples: South Dakota requires 30 hours per 2-year period, and South Carolina requires 30 hours including ethics. Since the point is the worker's own learning, an agent cannot attend in their place.
Arizona requires 10 contact hours of continuing competence per compliance period for certified PTAs. Several states track compliance through CE Broker.

AI slide and video tools such as Prezi AI and 2Slides already turn policy PDFs into in-service training decks and narrated videos. Vendors still advise human checking for clinical accuracy, so AI can only help prepare sessions the PTA conducts.

Under Article II, Section 2, confirmation requires the Senate's advice and consent. Committees hold hearings, review disclosures and FBI background checks, and the full Senate votes. Only the legislators themselves can cast these votes.
In NCSL's 2026 survey, about 55-56% of legislative staff said they use generative AI for research and summarization. Staff also said AI output needs substantial human review.

Sen. Bernie Moreno's office uses an AI assistant for vetting work, according to a secondhand aggregator report of his remarks. He also said Senate rules currently bar integrating AI into Senate systems.

AI and multi-agent systems in 2026 can extract, standardize and cross-check ESG KPI data. ESGAgent, for example, has tools for carbon calculation and checking alignment with regulations. This covers the data-gathering, tracking and analysis steps of program monitoring.

Research on agentic pipelines covers the whole ESG cycle: identification, measurement, reporting, engagement and improvement. It also notes that automation and continuous feedback are still immature, so a human still has to judge whether programs work and decide what changes to make.

Under CSRD the board approves the sustainability statement and auditors give limited assurance on it. Internal evaluation of program effectiveness does not legally require a human to perform or sign it, but external reporting does run through human approval.

Commercial electronic logbook software for power plants (Yokogawa eLogBook, MCG Versify OpLog) replaces paper control-room logs. It records events and compliance items, keeps audit trails and links to plant information, maintenance and lab systems. Some process data, such as tank dips, is still entered by hand.
MCG Versify OpLog logs events, activities and compliance requirements into a single tool and captures, stores and analyzes critical operational data.

Under Title V (40 CFR 70.5(d)), a designated Responsible Official, such as the plant general manager, must certify that compliance reports built from these records are true, accurate and complete. A human therefore keeps responsibility for signing off on the recorded data.

Current AI fitness tools use a phone camera to check a user's form and give feedback on lifts like squats and bench presses. That is coaching help after the fact, not a physical demonstration of the equipment.
AI workout coach apps record sets and show joint and angle overlays with tips, so they can support instruction, but a person or the equipment itself still has to do the demonstration.
Developers can build real-time vision agents that count reps and give voice cues, but these need the trainee to be physically present and moving, and they cannot adjust or operate machines.

Nomic's AI drainage-study review checks drainage reports against local criteria and flags mismatched drainage areas, storm events, pipe sizes, elevations and assumptions. It checks that documents are consistent but does not independently solve the hydraulics.
Arcadis is piloting AI with NYC DEP to flag inconsistencies and non-compliance in SWPPP reviews. NYC DEP staff keep professional judgment.

Local codes (e.g., Michigan, Kentucky, Georgia, Washington) require that a licensed professional engineer prepare and seal stormwater detention designs, and that a city engineer review the plans and calculations.

Compliance platforms like Vanta say they automate evidence collection, parsing and continuous control monitoring for audits through 400+ integrations, and cite an IDC figure of 82% less time per audit. Both claims come from the vendor.
A practitioner case describes building an AI agent to answer customer audit requests by gathering compliance evidence automatically.

Vanta's own guidance says organizations should not fully rely on automated evidence without independent review. Its comparison page also says a competitor's automation is brittle and non-deterministic, so a human still has to check the work, explain processes to auditors in walkthroughs and stand behind management's representations.

Cleanup cost estimating already relies on parametric software such as RACER. It produces repeatable, documented remediation estimates from available site data, with yearly cost-data updates. An agent could run this kind of structured estimating work.

In New Jersey, remedial cost estimates for NJDEP Site Remediation Program work must be signed by a Licensed Site Remediation Professional (LSRP). Other remedial work must be certified by a licensed Professional Engineer (PE), with the preparer's license number listed.
Ohio's brownfield grant program requires remedial cost estimates from a certified professional or engineer.

Commercial hazardous waste platforms (e.g., Triumvirate ADVISE, ERA EHS, ChemicalSafety) already automate manifests, waste profiles, pickup requests, return-manifest tracking and compliance calendars, so the paperwork and scheduling sub-steps can be handed off to software.

The generator, or the person acting for it, must sign the manifest certifying that the waste is properly classified, packaged, marked and labeled. EPA e-Manifest accepts electronic signatures, but they are tied to an accountable person's identity.

Under EPA's interpretation, the person who signs a manifest must have hazmat training under DOT rules. Signing is also usually done when the transporter picks up the waste at the site, which needs someone there in person.

AI demand forecasting in supply chains has moved from pilot to production at leading companies. The step from decision support to autonomous action is still in progress, and in the common model humans review and approve the agents' actions.
Gartner projects that by 2030, half of cross-functional supply chain management solutions will use agents to carry out decisions on their own. This means fully autonomous control is not yet standard.
Logistics analysts need no legal certification or license. Voluntary certifications such as ASCM's CPIM, CSCP and CLTD and SOLE designations exist, but nothing requires a human signature.
ReadiNow won a BCI Global Award in 2025 for a platform that uses autonomous AI agents trained in risk, compliance, continuity and incident response.
PagerDuty's Spring 2026 release includes an SRE Agent that investigates and resolves complex incidents at enterprise scale. Vendor sources say audit trails and human override are becoming standard.
BCP credentials such as CBCP and ISO 22301 are voluntary professional certifications. The search found no legal requirement for a licensed human to sign off on monitoring or resolution methods.
Microsoft's Teams Facilitator agent writes live notes, posts the agenda, runs agenda timers and records decisions and open questions. It is generally available with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license.
Cisco's Webex AI agents turn meeting summaries into action items, such as creating Jira tickets or scheduling follow-up meetings, and carry them out for the user.

Meeting-notes agents do not make decisions or invent commitments, and they flag unclear points for a human. Steering the discussion and settling stakeholder conflicts still depend on a human facilitator.

AI policy-generator agents (Lyzr, GeneratePolicy.com, ISMS Copilot) draft security and compliance policies mapped to frameworks such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 and GDPR. Their workflow still has a human review and customize the draft.

PCI DSS Requirement 12.1 requires a formal security policy that is established, published, maintained and distributed. Management endorsement is recommended and an assessor reviews the documents, so organizational sign-off stays with humans. The strategist in this task only assists, and no licence is needed for that role.
Policy ownership and governance sit with named officials such as the CISO or Treasurer, who approve the final policies and do annual reviews.

Itembase, launched in April 2026, is a game economy design workspace. It centralizes currencies, stats and items, models how players acquire and progress through them, and supports AI plugins. This means drafting and simulating currency and item catalogs can largely be done in software.

Seele AI generates virtual economy and in-app purchase designs, including currency sources and sinks and limits on inflation. It describes the output as a prototype for early design review rather than a finished system, so a human still has to review it.
PlayFab Economy provides standard catalog and multi-currency tooling. The agent can configure it digitally, and no physical presence or licensing is required.
AI 'synthetic user' agents, such as Adobe's UXCascade, now produce and gather usability feedback at scale. These tools can supply the evidence and arguments used to advocate for users.

In an April 2026 experiment, synthetic users diverged from real users, and the authors concluded the results can't be trusted without checking against real users. A human still has to judge and stand behind the user advocacy.
HF/E certification through BCPE (CPE/CHFP) is voluntary and private. It is not a legal licence, so no signing barrier applies to user advocacy.

Vendors such as dSPACE showed generative and agentic AI for SIL and HIL validation, test generation and automated CI/CD test pipelines at CES 2026. These are vendor claims. They show that test-case creation and SIL execution can be partly delegated.

In a Volvo/Chalmers study of generative AI for HIL test automation, only 23–36% of AI-generated test cases passed. Hardware-specific benches limit autonomy, so humans still have to review and run tests on physical rigs and vehicles.

US FMVSS uses manufacturer self-certification based on due care. No licensed individual is required to perform or sign system tests, but vehicle-level testing still relies on physical vehicles, test tracks and instrumentation.

Research from 2025–2026 shows LLM agents being used to build and run agent-based travel and traffic simulations that match standard benchmarks. The authors call the work preliminary, and multimodal networks and other complex settings remain untested. So agents can do the coding and simulation steps, but production planning models still need human checking.

Under federal conformity rules (40 CFR 93.122), network-based travel models must be validated against observed counts for a base year no more than 10 years before the determination. The task therefore depends on agency count and survey data and on calibration judgment. No search result showed that a licensed engineer must seal or sign model development.

An FHWA peer review found that many travel demand models give too little attention and effort to validation. This supports keeping a human expert to review calibration and validation before a model is used.

Autonomous research agents from 2025–2026 (OpenLens AI, Medical AI Scientist) run the steps from literature review through data analysis, coding and manuscript writing end to end. These are mostly preprints and have not been validated in peer review.
BioWorld reported two Nature papers from May 2026 showing autonomous AI agents working across the biomedical research cycle: forming hypotheses, designing experiments and analysing data.

Under 21 CFR 312, a qualified human investigator must sign Form FDA 1572, personally conduct or supervise the study, and ensure informed consent, IRB review and adverse-event reporting. Patient exams, biopsies and bench work also require a person to be physically present.

FDA has authorized autonomous AI systems that screen fundus images for diabetic retinopathy (LumineticsCore, EyeArt) and return results in under 30 seconds. Medicare pays for this under CPT 92229, so AI can already do part of the interpretation work.
Billing for OCT interpretation (CPT 92134) needs a signed interpretation and report written by a physician. The device printout alone is not enough, so a licensed human must review and sign.

Comparisons of retinal AI tools show that autonomous authorization covers only narrow screening uses tied to specific cameras. Most ophthalmic tests, such as slit lamp exams, tonometry, gonioscopy and dilated exams, are done in person with physical equipment.

Nebraska's anesthesiologist assistant standards list inserting pulmonary artery catheters and interpreting data from invasive monitors as tasks the supervising physician anesthesiologist delegates. That is hands-on bedside work done under supervision.

South Carolina requires a direct, continuous and close supervisory relationship between the anesthesiologist assistant and a sponsoring anesthesiologist, who is responsible for the assistant's activities at all times.

FDA-cleared AI tools exist for parts of the analysis, such as EEG trending and artifact reduction (Ceribell) and automated echo measurements (Us2.ai). They support clinicians' decisions but do not place devices or replace the clinician in the operating room, which limits AI to helping interpret the data.

Vendors sell wireless sensors that log fridge and freezer temperatures around the clock to cloud dashboards. They send text or email alerts when a reading is out of range or the power fails, and produce reports for inspectors. Where these are installed, an agent with dashboard access could do the monitoring, alerting and record-keeping. These are vendor claims I have not verified.

Alerts can be set to fire only when a freezer stays above a set temperature for a set time. That supports automatic detection of faults, but someone still has to be on site to check the equipment and fix it.

State guidance (Minnesota's sample plan, not the FDA Food Code itself) has the person in charge or a trained employee check product temperatures with a probe thermometer about every four hours. That is hands-on work, and many cafes have no sensors for an agent to read. Neither source requires a licensed human to sign the check.

In February 2026 athenahealth launched agentic patient-communication tools that give patients 24/7 access to front-office AI agents. Vendors also describe agents that sync patient information across EHRs, calendars and messaging platforms, which covers the routing, scheduling, reminder and status-update parts of coordination.

A 2026 industry guide places AI agents in administrative communication such as scheduling, referral and result tracking, and triage, and treats clinical judgment separately. A survey it cites shows lower comfort with autonomous AI beyond administrative tasks.

Under 42 CFR 482.13, hospitals must run a grievance process with set timeframes and written responses. The hospital's governing body must approve the process and is responsible for it, so a human stays accountable for grievance outcomes. Routine coordination messages do not need a licensed signer.

Upper's AI Dispatch software builds the schedule from the user's rules and gives a confidence score for each assignment. This suggests matching drivers to routes can be automated from a goal and a set of rules.
RouteNow describes an AI dispatch system that suggests truck and route assignments using real-time data. A human still accepts or adjusts the suggestions, and the claim comes from vendor marketing.

Wastehero's route software plans routes around vehicle capacity, time windows and road limits, then sends the plan to the driver. Assigning routes is digital work and needs no one on site. No search was run on law or licensing; no rule requiring a human to sign off on route assignments is known.

Grants-management platforms such as Appian, REI GovGrants and EY Grants Accelerator (FedRAMP-authorized) offer AI for compliance guidance, document classification and summarizing progress reports. This supports partial automation of the monitoring and reporting sub-steps.

EPA grant administrative conditions require recipient performance reports under 2 CFR 200.328 and route them through designated authorized representatives. A human official stays accountable for submissions.
State solid-waste grant forms require the applicant to certify deliverables and designate an authorized project representative. This means a human signs off on progress and compliance.

Joint Commission guidance says the bedside two-person check before a blood transfusion is done by a qualified transfusionist whom the hospital designates under professional guidelines and state law. A barcode or other automated system can stand in only for the second person.

Children's hospital policy requires the whole blood verification to happen at the patient's bedside with two people, a transfusionist and a witness, before the product is hung and the patient is monitored.

AI tools for spotting and predicting adverse transfusion reactions are still mostly research models. They support a clinician's decisions but do not replace physical administration or bedside assessment.
The AANA Scope and Standards say the CRNA must inspect the anesthesia machine and monitors before use and record the check in the patient's chart. The task is a hands-on, licensed one.
Automated machine self-checks have missed leaks and failures, so a clinician still has to do manual checks before each case.
Closed-loop anesthesia systems can adjust drug delivery, but they are device-integrated and still need a human in the loop. Software agents cannot prepare drugs or set up equipment physically.

The only AI paint-defect inspection systems found run on factory paint lines, not in collision shops. Nissan AUTIS uses fixed high-resolution cameras that take about 15,000 images per car, and technicians still confirm and classify each flagged defect. A software-only agent cannot use this kind of camera hardware or check a car in person.

Factory systems that pair AI paint inspection with robotic repair, such as EINES ESFI with AutoRepair, need dedicated inline hardware and robots, which are outside the reference agent's abilities. The task's other main parts, test-driving the car and checking fit, function and dimensions on site, are physical work by nature.

The search found no collision-repair product that does post-repair inspection end to end. An agent could only help in small ways: comparing photos or measurement and scan printouts against OEM specs, and drafting the QC checklist and records.

Medicare-certified home health agencies must use aides trained in a state-approved program of at least 75 hours, including 16 hours of supervised hands-on practice, and evaluated by an RN. The task is hands-on care that a person must physically do, but no rule requires a human to sign off on these chores.

The laundry-folding robots shown at CES 2026 (such as LG CLOiD and SwitchBot Onero) are general household prototypes, and reviewers found their speed unconvincing. They are robots, not software agents, so they are outside the reference technology anyway.

Robots that help with bathing have only reached early research, such as adapting an industrial arm to help with showering. Personal care still needs a person who is physically present and someone the patient trusts.

Bandwidth-planning tools and AI document-analysis tools for network architecture exist, but they give only rough, early-stage estimates. Sizing still has to be checked against vendor specs and measured traffic, which supports partial rather than full delegation.
Traffic from AI agents breaks the usual assumptions about peak hours and oversubscription. Requirements therefore depend on site-specific traffic data that sits inside the organization's systems.

A licensed professional engineer must certify the network design for some government-funded broadband projects, such as USDA ReConnect. For typical enterprise network requirements, no license or sign-off is required.

Vendors such as Opalite Health (YC W26) and No Barrier AI sell real-time speech-to-speech medical interpretation between clinicians and patients in 150+ languages. These claims come from the companies themselves.

A Boostlingo/Fierce Healthcare survey found most healthcare leaders accept AI interpreting for scheduling and billing, but far fewer accept it for emergency, inpatient or emotionally sensitive care. Their main concern is whether it performs well in real situations.

Under the US Section 1557 rule, a qualified human translator must review machine translation when the content is critical, technical, or affects a person's rights, benefits or access (for example consent forms and patient instructions).

AATA guidance says the therapist must get explicit written consent before using a client's artwork, including how the client wants to be identified, and must watch for subtle coercion caused by the therapist's greater authority. Choosing clients and getting their consent is relational clinical work that a human has to lead.
CATA/ACAT standards forbid publicly displaying client art without a dated, signed written release from the client or guardian, and forbid identifying clients in public.

Agentic event tools released in 2025-26 (Cvent agent Skills, Bizzabo, RainFocus Nexus) handle scheduling, vendor emails, RFPs, registrations and reminders end to end. These match the logistics sub-steps of a showcase, but hanging the work and running the event in person still need a human.

At Cleveland Clinic, the infectious-waste transport that does get automated is done by physical robots (AGVs) that move regulated medical waste to a sterilization room. Software-only AI agents without a body can't do this.
Research robots such as Siriraj Hospital's 'Wastie' use robot arms to lift and carry infectious waste bins. This shows the core work is physically handling closed containers.

A 2025 review of medical-waste technology says automation of traceability is still not widely adopted. Logging and tracking paperwork is the only part a software agent could help with, and it is a small share of the task time.
California BPC §1246 requires state certification to collect blood. Under the CDPH tiers, skin-puncture collection needs at least a Limited Phlebotomy Technician or CPT I credential.

The first FDA-authorized autonomous blood-draw robot (Vitestro Aletta, August 2026) is a physical robotic device. It does venous draws only, not capillary heel or finger sticks, and it still needs a trained phlebotomist to start and supervise each session.
Capillary dermal puncture is a hands-on skin procedure on the patient. Training programs teach it as a practical clinical skill, and a software-only agent cannot carry it out.

Remote management systems for minilab photo equipment have existed since the 1990s. They let a central site control how lab-shop processors run and manage production and quality, so some setting changes can be made through software.

Processors can adjust developer replenishment automatically from control-strip density readings. That covers part of the parameter adjustment, but these controls are built into the equipment rather than reachable by a general AI agent.

On a Kodak DKS digital minilab, replenishment rates are set on the machine's own chemical parameter screens, and some changes also require physically modifying the replenishment lines. That means a person usually has to be at the machine.
Automated cell culture incubation relies on dedicated robotic incubator hardware, not software agents. Vendors note its value comes from reducing human physical handling and contamination.

Automated slide preparation (inoculating, spreading, heating and drying slides) is done by specialised mechanical cartridge or robotic platforms. It needs physical manipulation, which a bodiless AI agent cannot do.

Lab automation for incubation means physical hardware (e.g., Thermo Fisher Cytomat incubators). An AI agent could at most schedule runs or look up protocols, which is a small part of the working time.

CodeSignal sells AI interviewer training. It runs simulated interviews with AI candidates, an AI tutor gives feedback on how each interview was structured and what to improve, and it is pitched as a replacement for live shadowing and as a way to certify interviewers. This suggests the training part can be handed off in large pieces.
CodeSignal's launch announcement says the training can be tailored to an organization's own scorecards, question frameworks and standards, so an agent could build and deliver custom training modules.

A vendor blog (marketing, unverified) describes post-interview reports on question effectiveness and recorded clips for peer coaching. AI can help with quality monitoring, but decisions about performance and staff and day-to-day supervision still need a human manager.

Cities such as Kelowna, B.C. and Abu Dhabi use generative-AI permit assistants that answer code questions and point applicants to specific code provisions. Kelowna says this cut early staff questions. These tools cover the 'explain regulations' part of the task.

A 2026 Florida League of Cities buyer's guide says AI permitting tools flag issues and cite the rule, but a person still makes the decision. In a Seattle study, the tools' compliance checks were about 87-92% accurate, so a human still has to review the output.

Local codes give the building official the power to serve notices of violation and stop-work orders. These must be written and signed by the inspector, so the authority behind the remedial requirements stays with a human official.

Ramp-design software such as K-MINE generates ramp geometry, grades and switchbacks automatically. That is the planning side, done by engineers. The operator's task is physically cutting, pushing and compacting material with machines.

Under MSHA 30 CFR 56.9300, mine operators must build and maintain berms at least mid-axle height of the largest equipment on elevated roadways. That is earthwork done on site. The rule binds the mine operator; it does not require a licensed individual to sign off.

Autonomous haulage changes ramp specifications, such as tighter crossfall and rutting tolerances. But ramps are still built by heavy equipment working physically on the ground, which a software-only agent without robotics cannot do.

Axon's Draft One uses AI to write police report narratives from body-camera audio. A human officer must review and approve each report. A San Francisco pilot used it for citations and misdemeanor cases.

eCitation software fills in citation fields automatically from a scanned licence and syncs the data with records, dispatch and court systems. A sworn officer still has to issue and serve the citation in person in the field.
No source showed AI report tools being used specifically by game wardens. For this occupation, AI exposure was described as limited to the documents around the field work, not the work itself.

Commercial AI tools such as BuildCentrix 3D Blueprint Takeoff analyze 2D drawings and pull out sheet metal dimensions and materials for fab shops. This covers the materials and scope sub-step. The source is vendor promotion published by SMACNA.

Civils.ai's AI duct takeoff produces only a draft from plans and schedules. The vendor says human QA is essential and the tool does no 3D coordination or clash detection, so a human still has to review the output before it is used.

In official trade descriptions, this duty means reading blueprints, sketches or specifications to decide fabrication and installation sequence and methods. That is mostly document interpretation. Field measurement is treated as a separate competency, and none of the sources says the plan needs a licensed sign-off.

A 2026 deployment of SkySelect's AI procurement agent at Magnetic MRO reportedly fully automated 79% of parts purchases through two-way ERP integration. Other platforms, such as AAR's Airvoyant, still keep a human reviewing recommendations.
CMMS systems track stock levels and automatically create purchase orders when parts fall below a set threshold, and some can send POs directly to suppliers.
Grainger accepts electronic orders through punch-out catalogs, cXML, EDI and an API, so a software agent can place orders with a major maintenance supplier.
AI tools draft OKRs and goals from a company's priorities, check them for weak key results and test how well they align. That covers the drafting and analysis steps of setting departmental goals.

Company law commentary, including Delaware case law and the views of White & Case, says AI can raise issues and make recommendations. Directors or officers still have to make and approve policy decisions themselves and cannot outsource that judgement.

Directors and their delegates should not rely on AI output without checking it, and they lose their legal protections if they hand their judgement over to AI. A human therefore has to review and approve policies before they take effect.

Job postings say ticket takers spend about 85% of their time greeting guests and scanning tickets in person at the gate. They also spot fraudulent tickets, check bags, and redirect guests whose tickets are invalid.
The role involves repetitive hand and arm motions to scan tickets and tear stubs, standing at entrances, and working in outdoor weather. It is a physical, on-site job.

Self-service scanning turnstiles and kiosks already check tickets and passes against the ticketing database without staff. That is fixed automation hardware, not a software AI agent, and staff still handle the exceptions.

Nail robots such as Nimble only scan and paint nails. Reports say they do not remove polish, buff, file or treat cuticles, so no machine does the soaking and orange-stick prep step, and software-only agents can't do it at all.
Nimble's device paints base, colour and top coats and dries them, taking about 10 minutes per hand. It does not prepare the nail beforehand.
Nail technicians need a state license almost everywhere, earned through 300 to 600 hours of training plus theory and practical exams, for example in South Carolina and Nevada.

Operation Lifesaver's RISC-LE rail safety course for law enforcement is mostly taught in person in 1, 2 and 4-hour versions. Some sessions are restricted to sworn officers, and the 4-hour version holds IADLEST/POST certification. That points to a human instructor delivering the course in person under a certification framework.
AI avatar video tools are marketed for turning police SOPs and scripts into training modules. This shows that agents can do much of the work of creating course materials.
A custom GPT for police academy instructors helps build scenarios, quizzes and presentations, but instructors still lead the training.
Exercising animals is physical work: a person leads, rides, lunges or hands the animal onto equipment. Even automated horse walkers need a human to load, tether or supervise the animal on site.
Programmable exercisers can run preset speed and direction programs for groups of horses. Software can help with scheduling and settings, but it cannot do the exercise itself, which needs a body.
Free-moving walker systems still need a physical work area and someone to watch the animals, which an AI agent without a body cannot provide.

Market Logic added a Persona Builder and Synthetic Panel to DeepSights Personas in April 2026. It includes an AI interviewer agent, and the vendor says new concepts can be tested across audience segments in hours.

Attest launched AI-moderated interviewing (Attest Explore) in June 2026. An AI research assistant drafts the interview guide, and an AI moderator then runs video or audio consumer interviews and probes for deeper answers. Similar tools include User Intuition, Conveo and Echovane.

Quantilope's August 2026 blog presents synthetic consumers as a complement to traditional research, not a replacement. Accuracy has not been independently benchmarked, so a human still has to check the findings and target-audience choices before use. The work is fully digital and needs no licence or sign-off.

IFS Softeon's Fulfillment Flow, launched in 2026, uses AI digital workers coordinated by a central operational agent across warehouse functions and nearby areas such as manufacturing line feeds. Human managers still set priorities and make the final decisions.

SAP's 2026 outlook describes role-specific planning agents (material planner, commercial, demand forecasting) that work together to recommend actions across sales and operations planning. The cross-department decisions stay with humans.
Agents now handle routine purchasing, generating purchase orders and suggesting transfers from forecasts, while humans keep strategic relationships and negotiation.

Third-party leaderboard trackers report that frontier models score about 95-96% on SWE-bench Verified (as of July-Sept 2026). The benchmark asks a model to write patches that fix real GitHub issues without breaking existing tests. These rankings were not checked against the official leaderboard.

Spotify built 'Honk', an autonomous AI coding agent that runs codebase and framework-upgrade migrations across thousands of repositories. It handles the edge cases that deterministic scripts could not.
