An MSR 2026 study of 33,580 PRs written by agents found that 2.66% contain reverting commits, ranging from 0.7% to 7.6% depending on the agent. A separate 2026 study says many agent-involved fix PRs depend on maintainers to merge them. Both point to human review still being needed before use.

Google's AI co-scientist is a multi-agent system that generates and ranks biomedical hypotheses, and some of its proposals were confirmed in wet-lab tests. It is still built to keep a scientist in the loop, and human checking is still needed.
Multi-agent tools such as SciAgents can build new hypotheses from more than 1,000 studies, but these systems are mostly at the research stage and are not yet routine lab tools.
Most biomedical engineering work does not require a PE license. A license is mainly needed to stamp designs or to testify as an expert witness, neither of which applies to research consultation.

AI tools such as Alongside's Kiwi chatbot, SchoolAI 'spaces' role-play bots and Gemini Gems are used for SEL and social-skill practice. These tools are run by teachers alongside regular teaching. Educators worry that AI could weaken relationship-building, and most of the efficacy evidence comes from the vendors themselves.
CASEL presents AI-powered tools as a support for human-centered SEL work, not a replacement for it.

Under ESSA Title I, paraprofessionals work under the direction of a certified teacher and may not be given full responsibility for instruction. No licence requires a human to sign off on teaching social skills.

Tools such as AbleSpace, SyncIEP and IEP Insight automate data logging, mastery calculations, graphs and AI-written progress notes once someone enters the observations. The direct observation itself still has to be done by a person.

The special educator decides what data to collect and builds the tools. The paraprofessional watches students in the classroom (prompting level, engagement, behaviour) and records the data on the spot with those tools, so physical presence is required.
Paraprofessionals give informal assessments and collect classroom behaviour data as the teacher directs. Accountability for the data stays with the teacher, not with a licence held by the aide.

Camera-based attendance systems that use facial recognition exist, including a reported rollout to 48,000 government schools in Assam. Without an installed camera, though, someone in the room still has to see which students are present. Research prototypes report roughly 85-96% accuracy and raise privacy concerns.

Under English school policy, schools must keep an attendance register by law. Class teachers mark it at the start of morning and afternoon sessions, and entries are kept for 6 years. This is a record-keeping duty, not a rule that a specific licensed person must sign.

In one New South Wales (NSW) school's procedures, the roll is printed weekly and the principal signs it to certify that it is accurate. The person who signs is the principal, not the teaching assistant.
Existing AI tools such as Orb Composer can harmonize and orchestrate an imported MIDI melody into a full arrangement. The user then edits the result, so a human is still involved.
AI orchestration tools turn a piano or melody MIDI file into a multi-track orchestral score. Voice-leading quality is claimed by the vendor, not verified, so an expert still needs to review it.

Copyrighted works need the rights holder's permission before they can be arranged, because an arrangement is a derivative work. That is a copyright licence, not a rule that a licensed human must do or sign the arranging.

Automated stainers such as the Leica BOND RX run IHC, immunofluorescence and multiplex protocols that users program. A person still has to load the tissue sections, slides and reagents, so the automation is in the hardware, not in a software agent.

Users can edit the temperature of individual steps in BOND RXm IF and multiplex protocols. An AI agent could help draft or tune these protocols, but the bench steps (fixation, sectioning, antigen retrieval, mounting) are physical.

Under CLIA, 42 CFR 493.1489, people who perform high-complexity testing, including histopathology tissue work under 493.1449, must meet set qualifications and hold a state license where the state requires one.
This federal fire job posting says crew carrier drivers must hold the state licence the state DOT requires before they are assigned, and they are subject to DOT drug and alcohol testing.
This posting says firefighters who drive fire engines as alternate drivers must have a commercial driver's license before the assignment.

At CES 2026 Oshkosh showed an AI collision-warning system for firefighters, not a driverless truck. The searches found no driverless crew carriers or fire trucks in service, and in any case the reference AI agents have no physical body.

Vendor pages for security scheduling software describe filling posts automatically. The tools check each guard's licence class, site clearance, training and overtime limits, then message the best-matched candidates. These are marketing claims, not independent evaluations.

Teambridge sells 'Security Operations AI' that matches available guards to armed or clearance requirements and contacts them to cover open posts. Its rule engine warns rather than blocks, so a supervisor can still make a judgment call, and each override is logged.

Guard scheduling is built around posts: each post has a location, hours and required certification. Putting a guard with an expired licence on a post is a regulatory violation, but no law found requires a human to make the assignment.

Electronic key control systems such as KeyTrak and Traka replace manual key logs. They record every key removal and return automatically, tied to the user's PIN, card or biometric, and produce an audit trail and overdue-key alerts.

Access control software like Genetec and Gallagher Command Centre manages cardholders and credential assignments digitally, including importing data and exporting card assignment records for audits. An agent using a computer can operate these tools.

Someone has to physically hand over the key or card and check the recipient's identity in person. Without an automated cabinet or reader event, the agent needs a human to tell it what was handed out before it can record it.

AI recruiting agents can work toward a hiring goal on their own: they source and screen candidates, schedule interviews and run adaptive voice or video interviews with scored evaluations. They hand control back to a recruiter at set checkpoints, and most companies keep a human overseeing AI-run interviews (71% say a human always oversees, 6% let the AI run the process alone).

Hiring security guards requires state-regulated steps that the agent can only coordinate. In Michigan, for example, the licensed employer must fingerprint prospective guards and submit the prints to state police and the FBI; in California, guards need DOJ Live Scan fingerprinting, training and a state ID card. The licensee is responsible for meeting these requirements.

Laws on automated hiring tools add obligations: NYC Local Law 144 requires bias audits and candidate notice, and Colorado's AI law provides human review of adverse AI-driven employment decisions. This pushes the final hire decision back to a human.
